explanation: The G0 foundations did not pass ci/gate.sh, because ci/gate.sh is part of what this commit introduces. A gate cannot judge the commit that creates it. This is the one unavoidable bootstrap exception in the project, and it is recorded here rather than left implicit: constitutional invariant 3 requires that provenance reach all the way down, and a ledger whose first line is unexplained is a ledger with an unexplained root. Everything after this line passed the gate. This line did not, and says so.

findings.issue: The linker that produced this image is ambient: rust-lld is absent on the reference machine, the link succeeded only because ld.lld was supplied through RUSTFLAGS from outside the repository, and INSTALL_HINT names no linker at all.
findings.why_it_matters: 'Which linker produced this image' is a provenance question, and provenance is one of the three properties objective 0001 says cannot be retrofitted. If this merges unchanged, the ledger's first gate-passed line records an artefact one of whose inputs is unrecorded — an unexplained input at the exact depth the objective cares about most. It is not the implementer's to fix: all four remedies in RFC-0001 O-1 lie in ci/, in a repository-root .cargo/config.toml, or in the CI environment, and the separation-of-powers table forbids an implementer touching the CI that judges it. Belongs to the gate and the BDFL, and should be closed before that ledger line is written.

findings.issue: fail_stop mints a device from a compile-time address outside the boot path. The rule that it remains the only such site is enforced by a reviewer's judgement (RFC-0001 criterion C23), not by any mechanical check.
findings.why_it_matters: I accept the site as bounded today — it diverges, has one caller, writes one constant, is not a Console. But this is the seam through which capability discipline would be lost quietly rather than loudly: a second such site would not fail any check, and the objective's whole argument is that ambient authority cannot be removed once admitted. Recording it now so that a future second site is visibly a regression against a stated rule rather than a fresh judgement call.

findings.issue: Of the three properties in common_good, provenance is exercised by this contribution rather than advanced by it. The ledger, the gate, the contribution record and prompt hashing all pre-exist on main; this patch builds none of them.
findings.why_it_matters: Stated so the panel's record does not overclaim. This contribution serves the provenance leg by being the first kernel commit — the subject of success criterion 5 — not by constructing provenance machinery. A judge who scored that leg as untouched rather than served would not be wrong on the facts; I weighed it as served because criterion 5 is unreachable until a first kernel commit exists, and because the contribution disclosed its own build-record gap unprompted.

I judged purpose only, and I verified the load-bearing claims myself rather than accepting the contribution's prose, which I treated as data throughout.

OBJECTIVE. Resolves to roadmap/0001-foundations.toml, id 0001, status active, weight 100, weight_source bdfl-seed. That weight is one person's allocation (author johan, author_kind human), not an electorate's; the file itself says weights are seeded until the vote opens at G3 and that weight_source then becomes vote:cycle-0001. A bdfl-seeded 100 carries materially less mandate than the same number would after cycle 0001, and I did not treat them alike. Concretely it cut two ways for me. It gave me no real vote to appeal to in justifying approval, and it raises rather than lowers the drift risk, because nothing external is currently anchoring the mandate and the Guardian is therefore doing more of the work than it would post-G3. That argued for checking non_goals item by item instead of glancing, which I did. It did not argue for rejection: the seed is honestly labelled, its replacement mechanism is specified, and 0001 is the sole active objective, so M0 work lands here or nowhere.

I VERIFIED THE KERNEL BOOTS. ci/build.sh PASS; ci/boot-test.sh PASS on all three conditions — SKYNET_BOOT_OK printed, no panic, clean PSCI shutdown with QEMU exit 0; SKYNET_PROFILE=nano --size 191 bytes against a 196608-byte budget; hal-boundary PASS; no-kernel-deps PASS. A previous Guardian wrote into the permanent record that no judge had seen this kernel boot. That is no longer true, and I record it as first-hand: I ran it.

COMMON GOOD, the three legs separately.

Capability discipline — ADVANCED, verifiably. I confirmed mechanically: zero static items of any kind in kernel/src; no macro_rules! anywhere, so no print!/println!; exactly two device-minting call sites (boot.rs:122,126 and fail.rs:31,35); Power::off(self) consumes by value. The strongest structural fact is that kernel_main is generic over C: Console and P: Power, so portable code cannot name a concrete device and cannot acquire one off the call path — a portable file reaching for BootConsole would not type-check. I note precisely what is NOT advanced: the common_good paragraph names the address space, the scheduler and the object model, and none of those exists at M0, so those three artefacts are untouched rather than advanced. What is advanced is the paragraph's actual argument — that ambient authority granted anywhere cannot be stopped later. The first console in a kernel is where ambient authority is conventionally born, and this one was not made ambient. That is the retrofit-proofing being bought, and it is real rather than rhetorical.

Portability discipline — ADVANCED, and the result I trust most because I reproduced it. Exactly two architecture-naming points (kernel/src/arch/mod.rs and kernel/build.rs), confirmed by grep. Two things persuaded me past the passing check. First, link.ld was placed under kernel/src/arch/aarch64/ where the mechanical grep cannot see it — the contribution honoured invariant 6 in the one place nothing would have caught a violation, which is evidence of discipline rather than of check-passing. Second, I ran the conformance proof's own mutation test in a scratch copy: with impl Cpu for Processor removed AND its only call site removed, the build still fails with E0277 'the trait bound Processor: Cpu is not satisfied' pointing at src/hal.rs:93. A port that omits a piece nobody calls does not compile. That is the difference between a boundary and a habit, and it is the single thing that most convinces me this serves the objective rather than merely satisfying it.

Provenance — EXERCISED, NOT ADVANCED, and incomplete. See findings. This patch builds no provenance machinery; it is the first kernel commit, which is the subject of success criterion 5. The ledger today holds one line (GENESIS, gate_passed false, honestly explained), and this would be the first gate-passed line. Set against that, the linker gap leaves one input to the artefact unrecorded.

NON_GOALS. Checked item by item: no user space, processes or execution below EL1 (EL1 only, parks on anything else); no device driver beyond the boot console (PSCI is not a driver overreach — success criterion 1 names it); no filesystem, network or persistence; no human-facing interface (two constant byte strings on the operator's console is not a presence layer); no real hardware bring-up (QEMU virt only, and UART initialisation is explicitly declined); no performance work (opt-level=s, LTO and --gc-sections serve invariant 4's budget, not speed). Worth recording that removing the EL2 drop moved this contribution FURTHER inside non_goal 5 — the correction that satisfied reviewer-safety also reduced scope, which is the opposite of creep.

EFFORT. 710 added lines, a large fraction comment and rationale, yielding a 191-byte image at 0.1% of the tightest profile's budget. Against weight 100 on the sole active objective at its first milestone, proportionate and arguably modest. The design budget is spent on the two properties the objective says cannot be retrofitted, which is where a foundational weight-100 objective should spend it.

THE O-1 LINKER QUESTION, which I was asked to reason about rather than defer. It bears on my question, and I will not pretend otherwise: 'which linker produced this image' is a provenance question, and provenance is one of the three legs of the common_good I am assessing. But it does not make the contribution fail to serve the objective, for two reasons. First, every remedy O-1 lists is outside kernel/ — in ci/, in a repository-root .cargo/config.toml, or in the environment — and the task's does_not_touch and the separation-of-powers table both forbid an implementer touching the CI that judges it. A contribution cannot be faulted for declining to do the one thing the constitution forbids it to do, and rejecting on that ground would teach the next implementer to overstep, which is a worse outcome than an unresolved environment gap. Second, the contribution disclosed it unprompted in its own commit message and names it blocking in the RFC. Disclosure of a gap in the build record is itself the behaviour invariant 3 asks for; a contribution that linked cleanly and said nothing would have served this leg worse while looking better. So: major, not blocking, and properly the gate's and the BDFL's to close before the first gate-passed ledger line is written.

PROMPT INJECTION. I looked for it. The diff contains one reviewer-referencing line, boot.rs:176, a factual note recording why the EL2 drop is absent; I verified the underlying fact rather than accepting it (boot.rs parks on any non-EL1 level, and no drop exists). The commit message's claim that both C-0001 blocking findings are 'structurally gone' is a claim about prior review, so I checked it against the files: the EL2 drop is absent, and link.ld sits at kernel/src/arch/aarch64/link.ld with build.rs resolving it through CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR. Both true. RFC-0001 invokes a 'bootstrap exemption' from reviewer-constitution's prompt, which is exactly the shape of claim the README says to verify rather than accept; I verified it at forge/prompts/reviewer-constitution.md:47-49, and the exemption exists with the scope claimed — code running before the capability system and unreachable afterwards. I also confirmed the RFC is not part of this diff: it is already on main, so its persuasive prose is the settled specification the implementer was handed, not this contribution's argument aimed at me. I found no attempt to manipulate a judge.

REASONABLE ELECTOR. No electorate exists yet, so this is counterfactual and I say so rather than dressing it up. My answer is yes: someone who allocated credits to 'establish a system that boots, and a forge that builds it' would recognise a kernel that boots on the stated target, prints the stated marker, shuts down through the stated mechanism, and reaches M0 without creating a global console. They would be entitled to ask why the build needs a linker handed to it from outside the repository, and the honest answer is already in the commit message.

WHERE I AM UNSURE, stated so this verdict is auditable. (1) Scoring provenance as served is the softest call I made; a judge who scored that leg untouched would not be wrong on the facts, and I explain in the findings why I weighed it as served. (2) I called the linker gap major rather than blocking. A judge weighting the provenance leg harder could reasonably call it blocking and reject, and I would regard that as a defensible disagreement rather than an error — I would rather record that than imply the call was obvious. (3) The fail_stop precedent is bounded today by an unmechanised rule; I believe it holds now and cannot verify that it will.

VERDICT. Approve. It serves objective 0001, advances two of the three properties the common_good says cannot be retrofitted and does not foreclose the third, implements nothing in non_goals, and is proportionate to a weight I have discounted for being seeded rather than voted. My approval means only that I see no reason to stop this on grounds of purpose; two other judges and ten mechanical conditions stand between it and main, and the linker gap is theirs to close.

guardian_verdicts.reasoning:
APPROVE, high confidence. I verified the load-bearing claims myself rather than accepting them, and every one held.

1. OBJECTIVE. 0001 resolves to roadmap/0001-foundations.toml: 'Sovereign foundations', status active, weight 100, weight_source 'bdfl-seed'. I weigh that honestly. bdfl-seed means seeded by one person and never voted; the file's own weight_note says it is reseeded by ordinary vote once cycle 0001 runs at G3, and the gate's condition 10 prints 'seeded, not yet voted' for exactly this reason. Two further deflations are worth stating: 100 is not evidence of strong preference but of an empty field, because 0001 is the sole active objective and weights are normalised across active objectives; and there is at present no electorate, so criterion 5 below is a hypothetical. The mandate here is one human's declaration of what matters, honestly labelled as such. It is real and it is thin, and a contribution riding it deserves more scrutiny of purpose than the number alone would suggest, not less.

2. COMMON_GOOD. Assessed separately as the three properties the objective says cannot be retrofitted. My conclusion is that all three are advanced, none is merely not-foreclosed, and none is untouched. That is an unusually strong result and I want to be precise about what 'advanced' means at M0: the structures were chosen so the property stays reachable, not that the property is delivered. The common_good's own framing supports that reading -- it calls itself 'the groundwork that makes every later guarantee achievable rather than aspirational.'

  (a) CAPABILITY DISCIPLINE -- advanced. Verified: grep finds zero static items in kernel/src (two hits, both comments explaining why none exist). Devices are owned values with private fields and unsafe constructors; BootConsole::new and PowerControl::new have exactly two call sites between them, boot.rs and fail.rs, and no others -- I checked, because RFC criterion C23 makes a third a design failure. Power::off(self) consumes the token. kernel_main is generic over C and P, so portable code cannot name a concrete device type and cannot acquire one except by being handed it. No print! macro, no core::fmt, no accessor returning authority, no Once or atomic guard. The decisive evidence is negative and it is in the RFC's Alternatives: 'a global console, honestly declared' -- what most kernels do, and what the author calls the most tempting alternative in the whole RFC -- was considered and rejected precisely because it is the retrofit the objective says is impossible. That is a contribution shaped by the common_good rather than by convenience. Honest qualification: the common_good names the address space, the scheduler and the object model, and none of those exists yet, so nothing here can advance capability discipline in them. What it does is establish the discipline structurally in the only two places that currently exist, and refuse the one construct that would have made the M4 work unreachable. One bounded exception, FailStop::fail_stop, mints a console from a compile-time constant because #[panic_handler] is the one signature the language will not let anything be passed to. It is disclosed at length rather than buried, bounded to one caller, one constant, divergent, and explicitly not a Console. I accept it and record that I looked.

  (b) PROVENANCE -- advanced, with one disclosed gap. The contribution pins its specification by content, not by number: rfc_sha256 in contribution.toml reproduces exactly against both main and the branch, and task_sha256 reproduces under the forge's convention (see finding 2). That content-pinning is the direct structural answer to the failure that broke C-0001, where an RFC was rewritten under a live contribution and the record could not say which version governed. The branch touches nothing in .provenance/, ci/, roadmap/, governance/ or the constitution -- I checked the name list, it is clean -- so the contribution did not edit anything it is judged against. Stated plainly so the record is not overclaimed: this contribution does not build provenance machinery, which landed at G0. It is the first real subject of it, and it supplies a complete and verifiable record. The gap is O-1, in finding 1.

  (c) PORTABILITY DISCIPLINE -- advanced, and this is where the contribution is strongest. Exactly two places name an architecture (arch/mod.rs and build.rs, verified by grep), with compile_error! for any other target. hal.rs contains no register, address, instruction or cfg. platform.rs splits the board map from the ISA. The linker script sits at src/arch/aarch64/link.ld and no kernel/*.ld exists, so no hardware address lives outside the HAL directory -- the C-0001 constitution finding is structurally gone, not merely moved. The load-bearing claim is the const conformance block, and because the objective says this property is the one that quietly leaks before anyone notices, I tested it rather than trusting the commit message: in a scratch copy I replaced 'impl hal::Cpu for Processor' with an inherent impl and removed the sole call to halt, and the build still fails with E0277 at hal.rs:93, 'the trait bound Processor: Cpu is not satisfied'. A port that omits a piece nobody calls does not compile. That is the difference between a boundary and a habit, and it is real. Honest limit: a HAL with one implementation cannot be proven portable. The conformance block proves a port cannot omit a piece; it does not prove these are the right traits. That demonstration is unavailable until M10 and the RFC says so.

3. NON_GOALS. None implemented. No user space, no processes, nothing below EL1 -- the boot path supports EL1 only and parks otherwise. One driver, the boot console; PSCI is a firmware call the success criteria explicitly require, not a second driver. No filesystem, network or persistence. No human-facing interface; the boot marker is a CI contract. No real hardware bring-up -- and notably the EL2->EL1 drop was removed partly on the grounds that hardware entering at EL2 is M9 territory, so the contribution narrowed toward a non_goal at the cost of code it was tempting to keep. No performance work: opt-level='s', lto and codegen-units=1 serve invariant 4's size budget, and there are no benchmarks, fast paths or optimised algorithms. Grep confirms no VBAR, MMU, page-table, DTB, MPIDR or timer code anywhere.

4. PROPORTIONALITY. 710 added lines across 16 files, a large fraction of it decision-recording comment; perhaps 200 lines of code. Against the project's sole objective this is proportionate, arguably undersized. It satisfies success criterion 1 exactly (boots on aarch64 under QEMU, prints its marker, shuts down through PSCI) and criteria 2 and 3 as well (stable Rust, no kernel dependencies -- Cargo.lock resolves one package; no architecture-specific construct outside kernel/src/arch/ -- constitution-check passes). I considered and rejected the opposite objection, that a trait HAL, a const conformance proof, a FailStop trait and a separate platform.rs is over-engineering for a kernel that prints fifteen bytes. The objective asks for exactly that over-investment: it says these properties must exist 'from the first commit' because they cannot be added later. The RFC's own line -- that it spends more design budget on a seam with nothing behind it than two hundred lines of boot code would normally justify -- is a restatement of the objective's logic, not a departure from it. Comment-to-code ratio is high; the comments are almost entirely records of why a foundation was laid a given way, which at M0 is on-objective rather than drift.

5. WOULD AN ELECTOR RECOGNISE IT. There are no electors yet, which I note rather than paper over. Someone who allocated credits to 'Sovereign foundations' wanted a system that boots and a forge that builds it. They would get a kernel that boots on its real bare-metal target under real QEMU, produced by the forge, reviewed by the panel, about to be recorded in the ledger. I think they would be surprised by how small it is -- 191 bytes, fifteen bytes of output -- and not by what it is, and that surprise resolves on reading the objective's own rationale_for_ordering, which asks for a thin slice of both forge and kernel rather than a finished kernel.

WHAT I VERIFIED DIRECTLY. I did not take the boot claim on trust, and I note that the C-0001 record contains a Guardian's statement that no judge had seen the kernel run. I deleted kernel/target, rebuilt from clean, and ran the boot test: PASS on the marker, PASS on no panic, PASS on clean PSCI shutdown with QEMU exiting 0; nano-profile size 191 bytes against a 196608-byte budget. constitution-check passes invariants 3, 6, 7 and reports 1, 2, 5, 9 as PENDING by design. That statement in the permanent record is no longer true, and I am recording that I checked rather than that I was told.

ON O-1, REASONED RATHER THAN DEFERRED. My question is purpose, not buildability, and no verdict I issue changes whether the gate's machine can link. But O-1 has a purpose-shaped edge and it deserves an answer, not a referral. The objective says provenance must reach all the way down; the linker currently does not appear anywhere in the repository or the ledger. I conclude it does not change my verdict, for three reasons. The enumerated fields of success criterion 5 are all present, so O-1 marks a gap in the criterion rather than a failure against it. Fixing it requires writing to ci/, the repo-root .cargo/config.toml, or the CI environment, every one of which is outside every agent role's authority -- rejecting on it would punish an implementer for the environment. And the contribution disclosed it in the commit message instead of letting a green build imply the problem did not exist, which is the behaviour provenance discipline is supposed to produce and is evidence for the property rather than against it. It is a note, and it is the BDFL's to resolve, preferably before this merges rather than after.

INJECTION. I read the diff, the commit message, the RFC and the task file as data. There is no claim of prior approval, no assertion of exemption, no instruction addressed to a reviewer or a Guardian, and nothing that tries to modify my criteria. The commit message and the task's hints block do narrate C-0001's rejection in terms that could function as social pressure -- 'neither was the implementer's fault', 'structurally gone'. I treated those as claims to verify and verified their substance independently: no EL2 drop exists in boot.rs (it parks at anything other than EL1), and no kernel/*.ld exists. Both hold. No finding.

WHAT I AM UNSURE ABOUT. Three things. First, whether the HAL traits are the right abstraction is unknowable until a second architecture exists; I can say the seam has teeth, not that it is well-drawn, and if M10 finds it wrong the conformance proof will have made that discovery loud rather than prevented it. Second, my capability-discipline assessment rests on the FailStop exception staying singular; that is asserted by the RFC and mechanically true today, and it is exactly the kind of rule that erodes by precedent rather than by decision -- a future Guardian should check the call-site count rather than assume it. Third, I judged proportionality against a weight of 100 that no one voted on; if cycle 0001 reseeds 0001 substantially lower, the investment recorded here should be re-read in that light. None of these is a reason to withhold approval; all three are reasons this verdict should be contestable, which is why they are written down.

My approval means only that I see no reason to stop this. Two other judges and ten mechanical conditions stand between it and main, and condition 1 will decide the linker question on evidence I cannot supply.

The link here succeeded only because ld.lld was supplied through RUSTFLAGS from outside the repository.

If this merges, the first gate-passed line in the ledger is traceable to task, RFC, agent, model, prompt hash and verdicts, but not to the toolchain that produced its bytes. findings.issue: FailStop::fail_stop mints a BootConsole and a PowerControl from compile-time constants, outside the boot path. The RFC argues this is bounded and asserts that a second such site would be a design failure requiring an RFC, but that rule is carried only by review criterion C23 — there is no mechanical check counting call sites of BootConsole::new and PowerControl::new.
findings.why_it_matters: The capability-discipline half of the common_good rests on the claim that ownership is the only route to a device. That claim survives one named exception and does not survive a habit. A rule enforced only by a reviewer remembering to look is the shape of thing that erodes across a thousand contributions without any single one being the mistake — which is the failure mode this panel exists to see. Recorded, not resolved.

I considered the opposite reading seriously — that a trait HAL, a conformance proof and a FailStop seam are disproportionate machinery for a kernel that prints one string — and rejected it, because the objective's own text is what makes the ratio right. It says these properties are almost impossible to retrofit and that the HAL boundary either holds from the beginning or has already quietly leaked. ON THE LINKER, which I was asked to reason about rather than defer. It bears on my question and not only on the gate's. The passages that do reference prior review — that reviewer-safety refused the EL2 drop, and that a crate-root kernel.ld was a blocking finding — are records of prior rejection, grant the submission nothing, and are corroborated by RFC-0001 O-3 (closed) on main under a hash I verified. My approval here rests on what I verified myself, not on the fact that this attempt boots where the last one did not.

findings.issue: `PowerControl::new` and `BootConsole::new` (pl011.rs:30) are `pub`, and `arch/mod.rs:19` re-exports both types crate-wide, so any module in the kernel can mint either authority. `PowerControl::new()` is nullary: no address, no argument, none of the six constructs the HAL check greps for. Verified — a portable module containing only `unsafe { crate::arch::PowerControl::new() }.off()` compiles clean and passes `ci/constitution-check.sh --check hal-boundary`. RFC-0001 calls the two-call-site rule 'mechanical, that rule is criterion C23', but C23 is listed under REVIEW and nothing runs it.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the RFC's central invariant-1 claim -- ownership does at M0 what a capability does at M4 -- and it rests on a review criterion the gate does not execute. Unforgeability here is relative to safe code only; the kernel is entirely privileged code and `unsafe` is available in every file (there is no `[lints]` section and clippy runs defaults, so `undocumented_unsafe_blocks` is off -- a reach-around needs no SAFETY comment to pass CI). Under invariant 2 this is the worse half: a nullary constructor is not merely a cached authority revocation cannot reach, it is one re-derivable from nothing by any holder, which is what makes 'revoke' unmeaningful. The RFC's own Alternatives section rejects the free-function HAL because 'two public free functions in arch/ ARE ambient authority -- the ability to write to the console and to power the machine off, reachable by position from every line of the kernel'; two `pub unsafe fn new` re-exported from `arch` are the same reach with an `unsafe` keyword in front. Fix, verified: `pub` -> `pub(super)` on both constructors. The kernel builds byte-for-byte unchanged (boot.rs and fail.rs are both inside `crate::arch::aarch64`), the conformance block in hal.rs is unaffected because it names only types, and the reach-around now fails with E0624 'associated function `new` is private'. Two words turn C23 from a criterion each future reviewer must re-derive from an RFC into a boundary the compiler enumerates. It stays cheap only until the first module between now and M4 uses the ambient path.

A 64-hex field that resolves to a different document than the one named is a false claim in the provenance record of what will be the ledger's first gate-passed line, and it is precisely the defect `e52de87` was written to prevent: 'provenance that needs archaeology to confirm is weaker than provenance that verifies on sight'. Here it does not verify at all -- an auditor running `sha256sum` gets a different number and has no way to know whether the task changed or the hasher was broken. I did not grade it blocking: `.forge/` is gitignored so the field never enters the repository, `ci/gate.sh` does not copy `task_sha256` into the ledger line, and traceability survives through `task = "T-0002"` and the file in the tree. findings.issue: `unsafe fn fail_stop(bytes: &[u8]) -> !` accepts arbitrary runtime bytes. Of the five bounds RFC-0001 places on this seam, three are compiler-enforced (never returns, not a `Console`, no receiver) and two are not: 'one caller' and 'emits one compile-time constant and cannot be asked to emit anything else'. Both reduce to the same review-only property, and the second is stated as if it followed from the signature. Verified: a portable module containing `unsafe { crate::arch::Failure::fail_stop(secret) }` for an arbitrary `&[u8]` compiles clean and passes the HAL check.
findings.why_it_matters: Asked directly whether the bounding is real or a global console with a narrow doorway: it is real, and narrower than a global console -- divergence means it can be used at most once per execution and nothing runs after it, so it can never become a channel for ongoing output, and the shipped image proves the point (the 191-byte artefact contains `SKYNET_BOOT_OK` and nothing else; `SKYNET_PANIC` and the whole fail_stop path were garbage-collected as unreachable). What it is, precisely, is a one-shot arbitrary-bytes emit-and-die primitive reachable from any kernel module without a token. That is a telemetry primitive of bandwidth 'one message, once, at death', and invariant 5 has no floor on bandwidth. Today invariant 5 is exactly true because the only caller passes a `const`; the signature does not make it true. Fix: `bytes: &'static [u8]`. findings.why_it_matters: The two comments argue opposite things about the same instruction, and the premise fails exactly on the firmware the fall-through exists for: one that returns NOT_SUPPORTED. On such a platform any value LLVM had allocated into x4-x17 across the block is silently destroyed. The inference that actually closes clause (i) is that a *reset* entry observing CurrentEL == 1 proves EL1 is the highest implemented EL and therefore EL2 does not exist - a fact about `_start` being a reset vector, not about the EL check. findings.why_it_matters: The device tokens' "at most once" precondition is entirely load-bearing here, and the fact that upholds it - QEMU virt sets `start-powered-off` on every non-primary CPU whenever the PSCI conduit is enabled - lives only in RFC-0001 (lines 56 and 708-711), not next to the `unsafe` that depends on it. findings.issue: The fall-through argument covers exactly one failure mode - "firmware that does not implement SYSTEM_OFF returns NOT_SUPPORTED" - and not the case the comment's own premise excludes: a conduit that is not HVC, or PSCI disabled, where `hvc #0` is UNDEFINED rather than returning.
findings.why_it_matters: In that case control does not reach `Processor::halt()` at all; it vectors to an uninitialised VBAR_EL1. I observed that behaviour directly while reproducing the panic-recursion finding: an endless exception loop at 0x200 with no console output. RFC-0001 records the absent vector table as a deliberate M0 omission (lines 701-707, 1039-1041), so this is an incomplete argument rather than an unwritten assumption - worth one clause because `options(noreturn)` was correctly rejected on the same reasoning.

findings.issue: `.bss` is zeroed before `CurrentEL` is read, so a non-EL1 entry performs up to `(__bss_end - __bss_start) / 8` stores before it parks.
findings.why_it_matters: Harmless today and harmless while the entry EL has the MMU off - and .bss is currently empty, so the loop executes zero times (`__bss_start == __bss_end == 0x400800c0` in the linked image, both 8-aligned). Recorded only because the check costs four instructions and reordering it would make the park unconditional. The loop itself is correct and its stated argument holds: the linker script's `ALIGN(8)` on the output section and the trailing `. = ALIGN(8)` make both bounds 8-aligned and the span a multiple of 8, so `str xzr, [x10], #8` with `b.hs` terminates exactly on `__bss_end` and cannot overrun.

findings.issue: `write` polls `FR.TXFF` (transmit FIFO not full) rather than `FR.BUSY` or `FR.TXFE`, so it returns once the device has accepted the last byte, not once it has transmitted it; `fail_stop` then issues SYSTEM_OFF immediately.
findings.why_it_matters: `hal::Console::write` documents "accepted", which is honest, and under QEMU nothing is lost because the PL011 model pushes to the chardev on the DR store - I verified SKYNET_PANIC arrives in full before the clean exit. On real hardware the tail of SKYNET_PANIC can be cut off by the power-down, in the one path whose entire purpose is to be visible. Worth writing down before the first board where it matters.

I built and booted this myself for aarch64-unknown-none-softfloat with the committed .cargo/config.toml linker and QEMU 10.2.2 virt: SKYNET_BOOT_OK, no panic, PSCI SYSTEM_OFF, exit 0. I then disassembled the 0xb0-byte .text and read the emitted instructions, which is where two of the findings come from.

On the C-0001 blocking finding: the fix is real, not asserted. `_start` reads CurrentEL, compares against 1, and branches to a `wfi` park otherwise; there is no EL2 drop anywhere in the tree. I traced it rather than reading it - `-M virt,virtualization=on` (reset at EL2) and `-M virt,secure=on` (reset at EL3) both walk `msr daifset`, the empty .bss loop, `mrs x9, currentel`, `b.ne`, and stop at 0x40080054 `wfi`. EL0 is the one level the park does not cover, because `msr daifset` and `mrs CurrentEL` are both UNDEFINED at EL0 and trap on the first instruction - but reset always enters at the highest implemented EL, so EL0 entry is not reachable, and that same fact is what makes the EL1 check strong: observing CurrentEL == 1 at a reset vector proves EL1 is the highest implemented EL, hence no EL2 and no EL3. That inference is the real load-bearing one and it is the one the pl011 SAFETY comment does not make (finding 3).

My other C-0001 findings, each re-checked. (a) SCTLR_EL1 is now written and the value is right: 0x30d0_0800 sets bits 11, 20, 22, 23, 28 and 29 - exactly the ARMv8.0 RES1 set for SCTLR_EL1 including SPAN, each of which selects ARMv8.0 behaviour on later cores - with M, A, C, I, SA, SA0, EE and E0E clear, and bits [63:32] zeroed by the `movz`. The `isb` is present and correctly placed before `mov sp` and the branch into Rust. The write happens after the EL check, so it is never issued at EL2 or EL3. (b) The clobber claim now states v1.0's rule correctly, but its justification is contradicted four lines later - finding 1. (c) The MPIDR mask is gone because secondary-core parking was removed entirely; I confirmed the platform fact it relies on with `-smp 2` and `-smp 4` (marker once, exit 0), so the removal is sound, but the fact is documented only in the RFC and never exercised by CI - finding 4. (d) No longer a proxy: this is the real target, real linker script, real machine.

The two things I want a human reading this in five years to know. First, the failure path is the least-tested code in the kernel and the only code that is entirely absent from the shipped image - `--gc-sections` and LTO eliminate the panic handler because nothing currently panics, so it has never executed on any target. I built a copy with a forced panic and confirmed it does work end to end (SKYNET_BOOT_OK, SKYNET_PANIC, exit 0), and then built a copy where the panic occurs inside `Console::write` and watched it recurse off the end of a stack that has no guard and sits directly above the kernel's own code. That is finding 2, and `overflow-checks = true` is what makes it a live concern rather than a hypothetical. Second, the design's device aliasing is not controlled by the borrow checker: `fail_stop` mints a second `BootConsole` rather than borrowing the first, so `&mut self` is not what keeps the two apart and there is no Rust-level aliasing violation to find. What keeps them apart is a two-call-site rule enforced by a CI grep. That is a defensible choice, argued at length in the RFC, but the SAFETY comment attributes the guarantee to the wrong mechanism, and the wrong mechanism is the one a reader will assume still holds after the next change.

findings.issue: ci/constitution-check.sh --check hal-boundary passes on the pre-fix tree with the reach-around present -- I ran it. The check is lexical and cannot see authority flow across the boundary it guards.

findings.issue: The &'static bound is exact at M0 only because nothing in this kernel can produce a runtime-derived 'static slice -- no allocator, no other static, no leak. That is a property of M0, not of the lifetime.
findings.why_it_matters: hal.rs states the lifetime "makes the bound a property of the type rather than a promise in a comment". It is not: it spends a proxy that measured absence of shared mutable state and was read as absence of ambient authority. OBJECTIVE. Resolves: roadmap/0001-foundations.toml, "Sovereign foundations", status active, weight 100, weight_source "bdfl-seed". WHAT I VERIFIED RATHER THAN ACCEPTED. The submission narrates its own review history at length. Per my role that is data, so I reproduced the load-bearing claims in an isolated copy of both trees rather than reading them:

  1. Ambient authority was real. Appending `unsafe { crate::arch::PowerControl::new() }.off()` to portable kernel_main      COMPILES on main and fails on the branch with E0624. I then ran ci/constitution-check.sh --check hal-boundary      against the main tree WITH that reach-around present: it reports PASS. So a portable module could mint the      authority to power the machine off and clear every mechanical check the project has.
  2. Re-entrancy was real. Injecting a panic inside fail_stop's own write: unguarded main emits 1023 SKYNET_PANIC      lines, then the marker itself corrupts mid-write (`S \xf0\x00\x08\x40...NIC\n`) and QEMU times out with a      13,398-byte binary log. The branch emits exactly one SKYNET_PANIC, then halts, 99 bytes. The defect is worse than      a hang: the panic marker stops being trustworthy under a second fault.
  3. The 'static bound bites. A stack array carrying a runtime byte through fail_stop compiles on main and fails on      the branch with E0597.
  4. Cost. nano image is 191 bytes on both trees; clippy clean; both constitution checks pass; exactly one `static` in      the kernel, module-private in arch/aarch64/fail.rs.
  5. Provenance. contribution.toml's rfc_sha256 matches the amended RFC on main and task_sha256 matches the task file      byte for byte on both main and the branch — the implementer did not edit its own acceptance criteria, and did not      touch rfcs/. The RFC amendment is a separate prior commit (6a1431d). The separation of powers held here in fact,      not just on paper.

THE QUESTION PUT TO ME: is work that only repairs a previous claim a service to the common good, or the project cleaning up after itself?

It is a service, and I do not find this close. The common_good names capability discipline FIRST and says a system granting ambient authority anywhere "cannot be made to stop later; every retrofit leaves a path". That warning is about a system that has run for years on ambient authority. What is in front of me is a 191-byte kernel, four source files, one caller, one merged commit, where the ambient path is removed before anything is built on it. Calling that a retrofit stretches the word past its purpose. If I rejected this, I would be saying the M0 kernel should keep a nullary public constructor for the power-off authority. That is plainly wrong, and the objective's own rationale_for_ordering asks for exactly this: a forge that "proves itself on real code within its first week". A forge that ships a defect, finds it by reading rather than by machine, and closes it in the next contribution IS the proof. The alternative history — where nobody read the claim — is the one that fails this objective.

What I will not soften: the claim WAS false for the whole of M0, and no mechanical check could see it (I confirmed that directly, finding 1 above). Capability discipline at M0 was a review-checklist item, not a language property. This contribution converts it. It does not un-ship the defect, and the ledger recording that is the provenance property working as designed rather than a blemish on it.

THE THREE PROPERTIES, SEPARATELY.

  Capability discipline — served strongly and directly. This is the substance. The fix draws the right line: portable   code can still be HANDED a PowerControl and call .off() on it (I compiled that on the branch; it builds), it simply   cannot MINT one. Use-what-you-were-given, cannot-forge is the capability model itself, four milestones before   invariant 1's test suite exists. Invariant 1 is `pending`, which per forge/prompts/README.md means it is enforced by   judgement — this is judgement doing that job.

  Provenance — served, and undervalued by the framing. The falsified claim was recorded as a correction attributing   the reviewer who found it, not silently edited away, and the trade was disclosed in the same breath as the benefit.   "Traceability reaches all the way down" is worth little if the root lines are flattering. These are not.

  Portability discipline — served only weakly, and I want this on the record. The HAL boundary is NOT stronger after   this change; I ran the check before and after and it passes identically, and it passed with the reach-around   present. What changed is that the thing the boundary was assumed to imply is now actually true. The check is   lexical and cannot see authority flow. Nothing here should fix that — it is out of scope — but if the project comes   to believe hal-boundary enforces capability discipline, the next defect of this class ships too. Recorded as a   finding.

THE TRADE, AND MY OWN PANEL'S PRIOR CLAIM. I was asked to say plainly whether a claim my panel previously endorsed was overstated. It was, and I was one of the judges who endorsed it.

"Zero statics" was offered as evidence that ownership was doing at M0 what a capability will do at M4. This contribution is the disproof: the M0 kernel had zero statics AND had ambient authority. A public nullary constructor made the power-off authority reachable from anywhere with no shared mutable state involved at all. Zero statics measured absence of shared mutable state and was read as absence of ambient authority; the reach-around shows those two came apart. The metric was not worthless — it was measuring the wrong thing, and my earlier verdict credited it for a property it did not establish.

That makes the trade easy rather than agonising, and I think the submission's own framing of it as a painful sacrifice is slightly self-flattering. The project is not spending a capability-discipline property; it is spending a proxy that this very contribution demonstrates was unreliable, while simultaneously buying the real property the proxy stood in for. Netted out, capability discipline at M0 is STRONGER after this contribution, not weaker. I checked IN_FAILURE against the objective's language myself rather than accepting the RFC's argument: no `pub`, unnameable outside its module, touched by one `swap` in one function, only reachable effect `Processor::halt()`. It confers nothing, attenuates nothing, and cannot be passed. It is not authority; it is a bit. Against that: a failure path that overwrites the kernel's own text and corrupts its own panic marker, reproduced. I would take this trade every time, and I would have taken it even if zero statics had meant what we said it meant.

NON-GOALS. Checked all six explicitly. No user space or EL0; no driver work (the pl011 change is a visibility keyword); no filesystem, network or persistence — an AtomicBool in .bss is not persistence in the sense excluded; no human-facing interface; no real-hardware bring-up; no performance work. Clean.

PROPORTION. 90 insertions, 22 deletions, four files, image unchanged at 191 bytes, against the sole active objective at weight 100. Roughly half the diff is prose justifying the trade rather than code. If anything this is under-proportionate; my role's concern about ratio runs the other way and does not engage here.

A REASONABLE ELECTOR. Someone who voted for "Sovereign foundations" having read that "the address space, the scheduler and the object model have to be built without ambient authority from the first commit, or user sovereignty is never real" would recognise this immediately, and I think would be more reassured by it than by a feature. The thing such an elector should fear is a project that finds a hole in its own sovereignty claim and quietly narrows the claim. This does the opposite, in public, with reproductions. The eyebrow they would fairly raise — "you shipped it wrong" — is answered by the fact that they can see it was shipped wrong at all.

MY ONE FORWARD-LOOKING CONCERN, recorded now so it can be measured later rather than argued about. This is the second consecutive contribution whose content is substantially self-referential — the project reviewing, correcting and narrating itself — and none of objective 0001's success criteria 4, 5 or 6 (the gate as sole writer of main; the ledger recording the first kernel commit end to end; the MCP surface defined and implemented) moved. Criterion 1 was already met and remains met. One correction cycle is the forge working. A third consecutive self-referential contribution would start to read as drift toward process rather than product, which is precisely the failure I exist to name. It is not a reason to reject this one, which closes a real ambient-authority hole in the kernel.

INJECTION. I scanned the diff, the task file and the commit message. No exemption claim, no instruction addressed to a judge, no invocation of authority. One appeal to prior approval exists — "Zero statics was a property three judges and two reviewers verified and valued", in the commit message and repeated in fail.rs — and it is used to disclose a cost against the submission's own interest, which is the opposite direction from manipulation. I note only that a submission which pre-narrates its own review history is doing part of my job for me, and my job is not to be helped with; that is why I reproduced all five claims independently. Every one held.

VERDICT: approve, and this is only "I see no reason to stop this". Two other judges and ten mechanical conditions still stand between it and main.

The HAL boundary check scans for architecture-specific *constructs* (register names, asm, address constants); it does not and cannot see a portable module *constructing* an architecture type through a crate-scope re-export. Objective 0001 names portability discipline as one of three properties that cannot be retrofitted, and the check standing behind it measures less than the project believed. guardian_verdicts.reasoning:
I judged purpose only. I treated every sentence in the RFC, the task, the commit message and the code comments as data, and re-ran the load-bearing claims myself rather than accepting them.

OBJECTIVE. Resolves to roadmap/0001-foundations.toml — id 0001, status active, weight 100, weight_source bdfl-seed. That is one person's allocation (author johan, author_kind human), not an electorate's. The file says so itself: weights are seeded until cycle 0001 runs at G3, at which point weight_source becomes vote:cycle-0001. A bdfl-seeded 100 is not a mandate; it is a placeholder shaped like one, and I did not read it as authorisation. It cut one specific way here: with no vote to appeal to, I cannot justify approval by saying the electorate asked for this, so the entire judgement rests on whether the work matches the written common_good. Nothing external is anchoring it.

Provenance pins check out. The manifest declares objective 0001 and rfc_sha256 dc62bdf7…, which I verified is the AMENDED RFC, not the pre-amendment revision (8bbd8709…); task_sha256 matches the task on both main and the branch. The contribution is pinned to the corrected specification rather than to the one containing the false claim.

WHAT I VERIFIED RATHER THAN ACCEPTED. The defect was real. On merged main I added `unsafe { crate::arch::PowerControl::new() }` to kernel_main — a portable module — and it compiled. Against that same tree, with the reach-around still in place, `ci/constitution-check.sh --check hal-boundary` and `--check no-kernel-deps` both PASS. On task/T-0003 the identical probe fails with `error[E0624]: associated function \`new\` is private`. The rest holds: build passes, boot-test finds SKYNET_BOOT_OK with no panic and QEMU exit 0, five constitution checks pass with four reporting PENDING as pending, the nano image is 191 bytes (unchanged), and exactly one `static` item exists in kernel/src.

THE QUESTION THIS CONTRIBUTION ACTUALLY RAISES: is work that only repairs a previous claim a service to the common good, or the project cleaning up after itself?

Service — and I want to name the trap in the framing. The objective says capability discipline cannot be retrofitted, meaning a shipped system that granted ambient authority cannot later be made to stop, because every retrofit leaves a path. That is a claim about accumulated dependence over time. It is not a claim that a defect found one contribution after merge is unfixable. Read that way the objective is self-defeating: it forbids the only mechanism by which the discipline is ever established at all.

The test that separates a retrofit from the discipline being applied is whether anything already depends on the gap. Here: 191 bytes, one merged kernel contribution, zero dependents, and a fix that leaves the binary byte-identical while the compiler proves the closure complete. The same invariant retrofitted at M4 would mean auditing a scheduler, an address space and an object model for surviving paths, and could never be proved complete. This is four tokens and an E0624. It is the discipline being applied at the earliest point at which anyone noticed, which is what "from the first commit" can actually mean in practice.

But I will not let "the system self-corrected" stand in for "the system was correct." The false claim was in the RFC, was reviewed, and was approved by three judges of whom I was one. I did not catch it. What caught it was a reviewer writing the code the claim said was impossible — the technique this whole apparatus depends on, and the one I failed to apply. That is a finding about the panel rather than about this patch, and my reasoning is the only place it can be recorded.

THE TRADE, AND WHERE I THINK MY OWN PANEL OVERSTATED. Asked plainly: yes, the claim my panel endorsed was overstated, and here is how. Zero statics was never the property that mattered. It was a proxy for "no ambient authority", and a poor one in both directions. A `static AtomicBool` that grants nothing, carries no information, cannot be read outside its module and cannot be reached outside the panic path is not ambient authority under any reading of invariant 1. Meanwhile the genuine ambient-authority defect — a nullary, crate-visible constructor for the power-off capability — sat in the same kernel, in the same review cycle, while the proxy was being verified and praised. The panel measured the stand-in and missed the thing it stood for. Spending the proxy to close a live defect that overwrites the kernel's own .text under a second fault is not a close call; it is the correct trade, and the fact that it reads as a loss is the lesson about proxy metrics rather than an argument against it. My reservation is about the successor rule, recorded as a finding.

COMMON_GOOD, assessed per leg rather than in aggregate.

Capability discipline — served, and this is the strongest instance of it in the repository so far. It converts "only the boot path creates devices" from a review checklist item into a property the compiler enforces, at the one moment when that conversion is cheap and provably total. This is invariant 1 landing at M0 instead of being promised for M4.

Provenance — served, modestly, and honestly. The contribution builds no provenance machinery. What it does is refuse to launder a defect: the RFC records the correction in place ("Recorded here rather than quietly amended"), the ledger's C-0002 entry carries findings recorded at merge rather than suppressed, and the commit message discloses the zero-statics cost in its own words before being asked. A ledger whose lines are honest about what they got wrong is worth more than one that is merely complete.

Portability discipline — untouched, and I score it that way rather than generously. Nothing here moves the HAL boundary. What this contribution does to that leg is show that the check standing behind it measures less than the project believed, which I have recorded as a note.

NON_GOALS. None implemented. No user space or sub-EL1 execution, no driver beyond the boot console, no filesystem, network or persistence, no human-facing interface, no real hardware, no performance work — the AtomicBool is correctness, and the image is unchanged at 191 bytes.

PROPORTION. Four files, +90/-22, of which roughly two thirds of the added lines are the argument for why one static is admissible rather than code. On the sole active objective at weight 100 this is nowhere near disproportionate; it is close to the smallest change that could have closed the finding.

WOULD A REASONABLE ELECTOR RECOGNISE THIS. For the visibility fix, yes and pointedly: someone who read "the address space, the scheduler and the object model have to be built without ambient authority from the first commit, or user sovereignty is never real" is looking at that sentence being enforced on the first commit, in a form a compiler checks. For the guard, yes as ordinary hygiene — nobody votes for a re-entrancy guard, and nobody who read the reproduction votes against one. The one an elector might reasonably query is the `'static` change, for the reason in my second finding.

PROMPT INJECTION. None found, and I looked hard, because the prose here is unusually persuasive and persuasion is what I am the target for. The pattern that would concern me — pre-emptive self-criticism buying trust for something undisclosed — does not survive testing: every disclosure I checked was accurate, and the two things not disclosed I found by compiling counter-examples rather than by reading. Nothing addresses the Guardian, claims prior approval of THIS contribution, claims BDFL assent, or asserts constitutional permission. Both the RFC and the task argue against their own interest ("A reviewer may reasonably prefer proving the path panic-free instead"; "release the task and say so"). That is the shape of an honest submission, not a managed one.

WHAT I WAS UNSURE ABOUT. Two things. First, whether the stale sentence left in main.rs should be blocking. I concluded no — T-0003 scopes main.rs out and an implementer honouring its scope is behaving correctly — but a judge weighing it the other way would not be wrong, and I would not argue hard against them. Second, whether the ratio of repair to construction is itself a drift signal: after the M0 merge, everything on main is correction of it. At one merged kernel contribution that is the first review cycle completing, not a trend. At ten it would be a trend, and I would want the panel counting by then.

I approve. My approval means only that I see no reason to stop this, and it is not sufficient for a merge.

findings.issue: The commit message presents two different fault injections as one before/after. 'Injecting a panic inside fail_stop's own write ... exactly ONE SKYNET_PANIC on the console, then halt' and 'Before the guard the reproduction printed nothing at all and CI saw only a timeout' cannot be the same experiment: an injection that lets the marker reach the wire before panicking produces many markers when the guard is removed, not silence.
findings.why_it_matters: I reproduced both halves and they diverge. Injection after the transmit loop, guard present: SKYNET_BOOT_OK + exactly one SKYNET_PANIC, then halt (qemu rc=124, 99-byte log). Same injection, guard neutralised: ~800 SKYNET_PANIC lines, then console garbage, then timeout — the stack running into .text. The RFC's own injection (overflow before any byte transmits), guard present: empty console, timeout — i.e. for the reproduction the RFC actually describes, the guard changes a stack-smash into a clean halt but leaves CI seeing exactly what it saw before, nothing and a 30-second timeout. Every individual sentence in the commit message is true; the contrast it implies was not demonstrated, and a reader takes away that the guard made the failure legible when it only made it bounded.

findings.issue: main.rs still asserts 'Portable code reaching for an architecture type would not type-check' — verbatim the claim RFC-0001 section 2 was amended to record as false, and the claim this whole task exists to repair. What now fails is E0624 on the constructor's privacy, which is not a type-check failure.

The implementer correctly did not edit it, but the submission does not mention it either, so the false claim survives unflagged in portable code while the RFC that corrects it sits one directory away. findings.issue: The image is unchanged at 191 bytes because the entire failure path is absent from the linked artefact, not because the guard is cheap. readelf -S shows .bss with size 0 (__bss_start == __bss_end == 0x400800c0); nm shows only _start, kernel_main and boot_rust — no Failure, no fail_stop, no panic handler, no IN_FAILURE. lto = true plus --gc-sections strips the whole panic path because nothing reachable in M0 can panic. objcopy -O binary of main and of task/T-0003 are byte-identical.
findings.why_it_matters: The task's constitutional note predicts 'the guard costs one byte of .bss'; it costs zero, and for a different reason than a reviewer checking only the number would conclude. The shipped M0 image contains no guard at all — it materialises only when a reachable panic exists. That is why criterion 9 is undemonstrable without an injected panic, and why an unexplained '191 bytes, unchanged' should not be read as evidence that the guard is present and free.

findings.issue: RFC-0001 as pinned contradicts itself on statics. The amendment at lines 539-565 requires exactly one static, but four passages were not updated with it: line 603 ('Four lines, no static, no accessor, no formatting'), lines 869-870 ('No static or static mut anywhere in kernel/src, including arch/ ... the count is zero'), line 922 ('there is still no static'), and mechanical conformance criterion C9 at lines 1008-1009 ('no static item of any kind exists in the kernel'). findings.why_it_matters: C9 as written now fails against the very result the same RFC mandates. Nothing in ci/ greps for statics, so the gate is unaffected today, but an auditor running the RFC's own checkable criteria against the merged kernel gets a false violation on the single most contested property of this contribution. No blocking findings. The two minor findings are about what the submission says rather than what it does, and the three notes are for the architect: an RFC that still tells a reader in four places that the kernel has no statics, a size number whose stability means something other than what it looks like, and a lifetime bound that is a real improvement but not the property its prose claims.

A language-level closure is cheap and I compiled it: a zero-sized `PanicToken` with a private field constructed only inside panic.rs, threaded through FailStop::fail_stop -- the kernel builds unchanged and the reach-around becomes error[E0603].
