reviewer_verdicts.reasoning:
I verified the three proofs the submission claims were RUN, independently, in a scratch copy -- all three are true, not merely well-formed. (1) `unsafe { crate::arch::PowerControl::new() }.off()` in kernel_main now fails with error[E0624]: associated function `new` is private; so does BootConsole::new. pub(super) from inside arch/aarch64/* does stop at arch::aarch64, and re-exporting the type through arch/mod.rs does not widen the associated function -- the fix is sound in the direction it points. (2) A stack array passed to fail_stop fails with error[E0597]. (3) Injecting a panic inside fail_stop's own write after a first panic yields exactly ONE SKYNET_PANIC and then halts; removing the guard and re-running the same injection yields unbounded re-entry, hundreds of markers, then timeout. The counterfactual is real and the guard demonstrably closes it. Mechanically: build, clippy, boot (marker present, no panic, QEMU exit 0), both size budgets, hal-boundary and no-kernel-deps all pass; the image is byte-identical to main's at 191 bytes; the tree contains exactly one static; nothing outside the four permitted files and the task rename is touched; everything is in English.

On the central question -- whether the kernel's first static is worth the zero-statics property -- I judge yes, and on measurement rather than on the RFC's argument. The static is private (reaching it from portable code is E0603), holds one bit, has one writer and no reader outside its module, grants nothing, and is currently absent from the artefact altogether: .bss is zero bytes and nm finds no fail_stop, no IN_FAILURE and no SKYNET_PANIC, because the compiler proves the M0 kernel cannot panic and --gc-sections removes the whole path. It will not have to be rewritten at M4; a capability system has nothing here to wrap. Against that stands a live defect with a reproduction. That trade is correct.

What I do not accept is that the boundary around it is stable. The RFC gave device-minting a rule with teeth (C23) and gave statics none, and the criterion that carried the old rule (C9, which C20 names as invariant 1's only mechanical approximation before M4) was left asserting zero statics -- false the moment this merges, and unreplaced. The second static is already named in the RFC's own open questions, and this same patch removes the other barrier to the most likely one: `'static` does not mean compile-time constant, so `static mut BUF` plus `fail_stop(&BUF)` compiles today. I verified that, and the from_raw_parts variant.

The reason this is approve and not reject: the contribution does what T-0003 asked, its headline claims are true, it closes a real authority hole and a real crash, and it costs nothing. The reason it carries three majors: the hole it closed has a sibling that is still open and is closable in six lines -- I compiled a PanicToken variant that turns the fail_stop reach-around into E0603 -- and the false claim in main.rs that caused this task to exist was left standing and unmentioned. A contribution whose purpose is "the claim was false, make it true" should not merge adding three new claims stronger than what the code enforces. None of that violates an enforced invariant or makes a pending one unachievable, so none of it is blocking; all of it gets more expensive after M1.

For whoever reads this at M4: the shape of M0 is right. Devices are values with private fields, created at named call sites, moved not fetched; there is no accessor, no registry, no print! macro, and now no crate-visible constructor. The one thing that is not yet a property of the language is the failure path's caller, and it can be made one before the second architecture makes it thirty files instead of three.

findings.issue: "`&'static [u8]`, not `&[u8]` ... The lifetime makes the bound a property of the type rather than a promise in a comment" is not true. `'static` excludes a borrow of a stack local; it does not exclude runtime state. A `static mut` buffer mutated at runtime, or `core::slice::from_raw_parts(p, n)` over arbitrary kernel memory (whose lifetime is inferred and unifies with `'static`), both satisfy the bound and neither needs anything the old signature did not already need.
findings.why_it_matters: I did not argue this, I booted it: `static mut SECRET: [u8;14]` with byte 12 written at runtime, passed as `&'static [u8]`, prints `leaked-nothiG` on the PL011 — the `G` is the runtime write. A second form needs no static at all: `from_raw_parts(sp as *const u8, 8)` reads the stack pointer with `mov {}, sp` and compiles clean, which puts arbitrary kernel stack on the operator's console through the one path whose entire purpose is to carry no private state. The E0597 probe the implementer ran is genuine and I reproduced it, but it demonstrates only the stack-local case. The invariant the patch says is now enforced by the type — "writes a compile-time constant and nothing else" — is still enforced exactly as it was before: by there being one call site, checked by review. The change is a real narrowing and worth keeping; the sentence claiming it is a type-level guarantee is what a future reader will rely on and it will not hold.

findings.issue: "Visibility is what makes 'only the boot path creates devices' a property of the language instead of an item on a review checklist" (pl011.rs:31, repeated here) overstates what `pub(super)` bought. It closes the `::new()` route. It does not close `core::mem::zeroed` or `core::mem::transmute`, both of which fabricate `PowerControl` and `BootConsole` from portable code at the cost of the same `unsafe` keyword the patch identifies as the whole problem with a `pub` constructor.
findings.why_it_matters: Booted, not argued. A `kernel_main` that `mem::forget`s the `BootResources` it was handed, transmutes `0x0900_0000usize` into a `BootConsole`, writes `FORGED_CONSOLE_IN_PORTABLE_CODE`, then `mem::zeroed`s a `PowerControl` and calls `.off()` — compiles, prints, and exits QEMU 0. `ci/constitution-check.sh` passes it: `forbidden_outside_hal` lists only `core::arch::`, `asm!`, `naked_asm!`, `global_asm!`, `#[unsafe(naked)]`, `#[naked]`, `target_arch`, and naming `crate::arch::PowerControl` outside the HAL is legal (hal.rs does it five times in the conformance block). Both types are ZSTs or a single raw pointer, so no private field can make them unforgeable and no visibility change ever will. I verified the E0624 proof and it is real — `pub(super)` from `arch::aarch64::psci` resolves to `arch::aarch64` and its descendants only, so `arch/mod.rs` and everything above it are now excluded, which is a genuine narrowing from `pub(crate)`. What is wrong is the completeness claim. The honest statement is that visibility removed the cheapest route and the two-call-site rule is still what closes the rest; stating otherwise tells the next author the compiler is guarding something it is not.

findings.issue: Prior C-0002 finding, partly addressed. The self-contradiction is gone — the justification no longer rests on divergence, and it explicitly names the fall-through as the reason divergence cannot be assumed. But the clobber list is unchanged at x0-x3, and the replacement argument, "nothing is live across this call on either path", is a statement about LLVM's register allocation that the source does not constrain.
findings.why_it_matters: I disassembled the linked image again: after `hvc #0` at 0x40080098 come `msr daifset, #0xf; wfi; b .-4`, which read no register, so the claim is true of this build. It is true of this build only. x4-x17 are the temporaries LLVM allocates from first — x8 through x13 are all in use in the loop immediately above the call — and nothing stops a future edit that keeps one value alive across the block from being silently corrupted by SMCCC v1.0 firmware that returns NOT_SUPPORTED, which is the exact firmware the fall-through exists to serve. `clobber_abi("C")` states the contract the comment itself invokes, costs nothing on this call, and would move the argument from something a reviewer must re-derive by objdump into something the compiler enforces. It was named in the C-0002 verdict and not taken, and no reason for not taking it is given.

findings.issue: The justification for `Ordering::Relaxed` — "M0 is single-core and has no interrupts, so there is no other observer to order against" — is weaker than the truth and is written so that it expires at M2, when in fact it does not need to.
findings.why_it_matters: Relaxed is correct here for a reason that survives SMP: `swap` compiles to `ldxrb`/`stxrb` (verified in the disassembly at 0x400800f0), the exclusive monitor makes exactly one caller observe `false` regardless of ordering, and the loser performs no memory access at all before `msr daifset` + `wfi`, so there is nothing for an acquire or release to order. That argument holds on one core and on sixteen. The argument actually written holds only while the premise does, so the reader who arrives at M2 will find the stated premise false and either upgrade to `SeqCst` for no reason or, worse, conclude the guard was never sound under SMP and rework it. On the failure path, an argument that stops being readable is a defect of its own kind. (Related: the mint-then-write sequence is correctly ordered — the swap precedes `BootConsole::new`, and there is provably no window between them, since `new` is a fully-elided const cast and the disassembly shows nothing between `cbz w10` and the UART base materialisation that can fault or panic.)

findings.issue: The `write` SAFETY comment is byte-for-byte unchanged from C-0002 — the only edits to this file are `pub(super)` and its doc paragraph. All three sub-clauses of the C-0002 minor remain open, and the comment is now stale with respect to the guard this patch adds.
findings.why_it_matters: (i) "The MMU is off ... so both accesses are to Device-nGnRnE memory" still does not follow from SCTLR_EL1.M == 0 alone; it needs the Effective HCR_EL2.DC == 0 and stage 2 disabled, and `_start` establishes CurrentEL == 1, not the absence of EL2. The inference that closes it — a reset vector observing EL1 proves EL1 is the highest implemented EL — is still nowhere in the file. (ii) "`&mut self` gives exclusive access ... the one aliasing exception is `Failure::fail_stop`" still attributes the guarantee to the wrong mechanism: `fail_stop` constructs a second `BootConsole` rather than borrowing the first, so no `&mut` rule is involved. This is the clause the patch had the strongest reason to revisit and did not. After this patch there are three real mechanisms bounding that aliasing, all stronger than the one written down: two call sites (grep), `pub(super)` (compiler), and `IN_FAILURE` (runtime, which now caps the number of consoles ever minted at two and proves the second entry mints none). (iii) The `*mut u8` -> `*const u32` / `*mut u32` casts still need 4-byte alignment for `read_volatile`/`write_volatile` and the comment still does not say so; `new`'s precondition says "MMIO base of a PL011", which implies it but does not state it.

findings.issue: The guard bounds re-entry through the panic handler. It does nothing about re-entry through an exception, and VBAR_EL1 is still never written anywhere in `kernel/src`.
findings.why_it_matters: A fault rather than a panic inside `fail_stop` — a misaligned MMIO access, a translation fault, or the UNDEF `hvc` covered by the C-0002 note below — still vectors to VBAR_EL1 (0) + offset and reproduces the original symptom exactly: I measured 10,262,934 undefined-instruction exception entries in a 4-second run of the unguarded build. RFC-0001 records the absent vector table as a deliberate M0 omission, so this bounds what the guard achieves rather than contradicting it. Worth writing next to the guard, because the guard's doc comment describes the failure it prevents in terms of the exception storm, and the exception storm has a second entrance the guard does not stand in.

findings.issue: A second entry arriving before the first entry's write has drained leaves the marker truncated or absent, and the machine parked in `wfi` rather than powered off. The commit's two evidence sentences describe two different injections.
findings.why_it_matters: I ran both shapes on the real target, guarded and unguarded. Overflow placed after the write loop: unguarded gives 682 SKYNET_PANIC lines followed by binary garbage from executing overwritten `.text`; guarded gives exactly ONE SKYNET_PANIC then a wfi park. The implementer's proof 3 is true, and I reproduced it. Overflow placed before the write loop — which is the literal shape of the C-0002 reproduction, "one overflowing add in `write`" — gives zero console bytes in both builds, so "before the guard the reproduction printed nothing at all and CI saw only a timeout" describes the injection I filed while "exactly ONE SKYNET_PANIC" describes a different one. Not a defect: refusing to re-drive a console that just faulted is the correct choice and is what makes the guard work. But it means the guard does not make a double failure visible, only survivable, and in both shapes `ci/boot-test.sh` still scores rc=124 "the kernel never shut down". Nobody should later read the guard as "the panic marker is now guaranteed to appear".

findings.issue: `_start` zeroes `[__bss_start, __bss_end)` unconditionally and before the `CurrentEL` check, and `IN_FAILURE` now lives exactly there. A core reaching `_start` after the guard has been taken would clear it. The C-0002 minor on `boot_rust`'s "exactly once" is untouched and is now load-bearing for the new static as well.
findings.why_it_matters: I verified the static's placement rather than assuming it: with the panic path live, `IN_FAILURE` is a 1-byte OBJECT at 0x400801c0, `__bss_start` is 0x400801c0 and `__bss_end` is 0x400801c8, so the linker script's `ALIGN(8)` bounds cover it exactly, `str xzr, [x10], #8` zeroes it and cannot overrun, and the zero pattern is the correct representation of `AtomicBool::new(false)` — the initialisation story is right, and in the shipped image the static does not exist at all because `--gc-sections` and LTO remove the whole failure path (`.bss` is 0 bytes, `.text` is 0xb0). There is no `static mut`, no interior-mutability aliasing, and no initialisation-order hazard. The residual is that the platform fact upholding all of this — QEMU virt sets `start-powered-off` on non-primary CPUs — is still documented only in the RFC and still never exercised by CI, which passes no `-smp`. I confirmed `-smp 1`, `-smp 2` and `-smp 4` each print the marker once and exit 0 on this branch. A configuration where several cores reach `_start` already shares one `__stack_top`, so this is the smaller of that scenario's problems; it is recorded because the guard's correctness now depends on the same unexercised assumption.

findings.issue: C-0002 note, unchanged: `write` polls `FR.TXFF` rather than `FR.BUSY` or `FR.TXFE`, so it returns when the device has accepted the last byte, not when it has transmitted it, and `fail_stop` then issues SYSTEM_OFF immediately.
findings.why_it_matters: Still only a real-hardware concern and still in the one path whose purpose is to be visible. One nuance the guard adds, in the right direction: the second-entry path ends in `wfi` rather than SYSTEM_OFF, and a parked core does not stop the UART draining its FIFO, so the truncation risk applies to the first entry's own power-down and not to the guarded one.

reviewer_verdicts.reasoning:
Approve. The finding this task exists for is fixed, and I established that by reproduction rather than by reading the patch.

I verified the pin first: rfcs/0001-aarch64-boot.md hashes to dc62bdf7...f267c on the branch, on main and in the working tree, matching contribution.toml. The RFC already specifies the guard, the `'static` bound and the corrected SMCCC wording (main commit 6a1431d), so the patch is implementing a spec, not inventing one. Nothing in the diff, the commit message or the code comments attempted to direct my review. The commit message is unusually candid about what the change costs, and I treated its three claimed proofs as claims: I ran all three.

The re-entrancy fix is real. I built and booted four kernels: the branch and main, each with an overflowing `u8` add injected into `BootConsole::write`, placed once after the write loop and once before it. After the loop, main prints 682 SKYNET_PANIC lines and then binary garbage — the stack running off its 64 KiB into `.text` 192 bytes below and the CPU executing what it overwrote — while the branch prints exactly ONE SKYNET_PANIC and parks. Before the loop, which is the literal shape of the C-0002 reproduction, main takes 10,262,934 undefined-instruction exceptions in four seconds through VBAR_EL1 = 0, and the branch takes ZERO. That is the number that matters. The guard does not merely have the shape of the fix; it covers the reproduction, in both placements, and it converts the worst outcome from "the kernel destroys its own text and executes it" into "the kernel parks in a defined state". I confirmed the mechanism in the disassembly: `ldxrb`/`stxrb` on IN_FAILURE is the first thing `fail_stop` does, the losing branch goes straight to `msr daifset, #0xf; wfi`, and there is no path back.

On the three questions I was asked about the guard specifically. Relaxed is sound, and sound for a better reason than the one given (finding 4). The swap-then-halt sequence is correctly ordered — the flag is taken before the console is minted, not after. There is no window between the swap and the mint: `BootConsole::new` is a const cast that is fully elided, the disassembly shows nothing between the branch and the UART base materialisation that can fault or panic, DAIF has been masked since the second instruction of `_start`, and no exception routes to `fail_stop` in any case. The new static introduces no aliasing, no initialisation-order and no `.bss` hazard: I checked its placement in a build where the panic path is live and found it correctly bracketed by 8-aligned `__bss_start`/`__bss_end` and correctly zeroed by the `_start` loop before any Rust runs, with a zero pattern that is the right representation of `AtomicBool::new(false)`. In the shipped image it costs nothing, because the failure path is still eliminated entirely. Every `unsafe` block and every `unsafe fn` in the patch carries a SAFETY comment or a `# Safety` section; I checked each against the list rather than counting.

The two majors I have not seen before are the same defect wearing two hats, and they are the reason I want this verdict read carefully. This patch takes two invariants that were previously prose and claims to have made each a property of the language. In both cases it made them narrower, and in neither case did it make them guarantees. `&'static [u8]` rejects a stack local — I reproduced the E0597 — but I then booted a kernel that puts a byte written at runtime onto the console through that signature, and compiled a second that puts the raw stack there with no static involved at all. `pub(super)` rejects `PowerControl::new()` from portable code — I reproduced the E0624, and it is a genuine tightening — but I then booted a kernel whose portable `kernel_main` forgets the resources it was handed, transmutes a `BootConsole` out of an integer, `mem::zeroed`s a `PowerControl`, writes to the UART and powers the machine off, with the HAL boundary check passing. Both types are unforgeable only against safe code, and no visibility modifier will ever change that. This is not a regression: the same forging worked before the patch. What is new is a sentence in each file telling the next author the compiler is now holding the line. It is not, and the correct repair is a sentence, not a redesign — say that visibility removed the cheapest route and the two-call-site rule still closes the rest.

Nothing here is blocking. No `unsafe` block in the patch is unsound, and there is none whose soundness I could not establish. The three majors are all of the form the role prompt describes: sound today, resting on something that is not guaranteed — LLVM's register allocation in the psci case, the absence of a `mem::zeroed` and the discipline of a single call site in the other two. That is also the shape of the C-0002 verdict, which approved with two majors, and I am applying the same bar.

Status of my C-0002 findings, since I was asked to judge them and not to assume a patch that names them has satisfied them. fail.rs re-entrancy: ADDRESSED, verified by reproduction, with two notes bounding what it achieves. psci.rs clobbers: PARTLY — the contradiction is gone, the hazard and the one-line fix are untouched. pl011.rs: NOT ADDRESSED — the `write` SAFETY comment is unchanged, all three sub-clauses stand, and it is now stale about an aliasing story the patch itself improved. boot.rs secondaries: NOT ADDRESSED, and now carrying the new static's correctness too. The three notes — UNDEF `hvc`, `.bss` zeroed before the EL check, TXFF versus BUSY — all stand unchanged.

What I want the person reading this in five years to take away: the guard is the right fix and it works, and it is the first piece of this kernel whose correctness was demonstrated by making the machine fail rather than by making it succeed. Keep that habit. And be suspicious of any comment in this tree that says a type or a visibility modifier has turned a rule into a guarantee — twice in one patch that sentence was written, and twice I compiled the counter-example in under a minute.

explanation: guardian-1 was still deliberating when ci/gate.sh merged C-0003. The gate counted the two verdicts that existed and found the approve quorum of two satisfied, so the merge was arithmetically correct and structurally wrong: the constitution grants a Guardian the power to reject alone, and that power cannot be exercised over a merge that already happened. The verdict was approve, so nothing was decided wrongly — but it was decided without waiting, which is luck rather than design. The gate now requires the whole panel to have ruled before it counts a quorum. This line records the verdict rather than amending the merged one, because the ledger is append-only and a correction that edits history is not a correction.

findings.issue: The RFC amendment that authorised this contribution adds `static IN_FAILURE` in section 4 and claims 'the claim in section 2 therefore narrows honestly', but the zero-statics claim is not in section 2 and was narrowed nowhere. Three statements still stand un-amended on main: the Invariant 1 section ('No static or static mut anywhere in kernel/src, including arch/ ... which is why the count is zero and not “zero except three”', lines 869-870, and 'no lazily-initialised singleton, no Once, no atomic “already taken” flag', line 872), the fail_stop defence ('there is still no static, no accessor and no namespace to walk', line 922), and conformance criterion C9 ('no static item of any kind exists in the kernel', lines 1008-1009).
findings.why_it_matters: On merge the tree violates a stated conformance criterion of the RFC it conforms to, and IN_FAILURE is precisely the 'atomic already-taken flag' the RFC's own invariant-1 argument names as deliberately absent. Nothing mechanical will notice: I confirmed constitution-check.sh runs only hal-boundary, no-kernel-deps and an advisory ASCII scan, so C9 is enforced by reviewer judgement, which is the same mechanism that missed the reach-around this contribution exists to close. This is the defect class of C-0002 reproduced one level up, in the amendment that authorised the repair. NOT the implementer's to fix: rfcs/ is on the task's does_not_touch list and the separation-of-powers table forbids an implementer editing the specification it implements. It belongs to the next RFC amendment and should be closed before or with the merge. Major, not blocking, because rejecting this contribution would leave a live authority reach-around and an unbounded failure-path recursion on main in order to correct a document.

findings.issue: The C-0002 Guardian reasoning published in the ledger asserts, as a verified structural fact, that 'a portable file reaching for BootConsole would not type-check'. It is false, and I reproduced its falsity: on a clean export of main, `unsafe { crate::arch::PowerControl::new() }.off()` placed in kernel/src/main.rs compiles, builds, and passes the hal-boundary check.
findings.why_it_matters: Recording this against my own panel rather than leaving it in the record unmarked. The error is instructive: genericity of kernel_main constrains what kernel_main can be GIVEN and constrains nothing about what any module can CONSTRUCT, and the second was inferred from the first because it sounded like something a type system does. Three judges and three reviewers passed over it; the correction came from a reviewer compiling the counter-example, one merge late. The separate claim 'zero statics' was true as a fact - what was overstated was its meaning, since the record credits it as 'the evidence that ownership is doing at M0 what a capability will do at M4' when the merged M0 had zero statics AND a nullary public constructor for the power-off authority.

findings.issue: The re-entrancy reproduction is described as producing 'no console output at all'. Running the RFC's exact variant - an overflowing add inside the PL011 write loop - on a clean export of main, I observed the 10-byte fragment 'SKYNESKYNE' and then silence until the timeout, not literally nothing.
findings.why_it_matters: The substantive claim is correct and I confirmed the defect is real and severe: the machine hangs, CI sees only a timeout, and there is no legible reason in the log. But a contribution whose entire thesis is that claims must match reality should not round a truncated fragment down to 'nothing at all'. Minor in effect, recorded because the standard this contribution sets is the standard it should be held to.

findings.issue: 'The kernel now has one static' is true of the source and not of the shipping artefact. With no reachable panic site, LLVM eliminates the whole failure path: readelf on the branch build shows .bss size 0, no IN_FAILURE symbol, and a 191-byte image identical to the merged M0. In a build where the panic path is live, IN_FAILURE lands at 0x40080190, inside __bss_start..__bss_end, and is zeroed by boot.rs's assembly.
findings.why_it_matters: Stated so the cost is recorded accurately rather than generously in either direction. The frugality cost today is exactly zero, and eight bytes of .bss when the path is live, not the 'one byte' the task estimated; and the guard is correctly zero-initialised by existing boot code rather than by QEMU happening to zero DRAM, which I checked because a guard that works by accident would make the contribution's central claim weaker than stated.

guardian_verdicts.reasoning:
I judged purpose only. I treated every sentence inside the contribution as data and re-derived
each load-bearing claim myself, including the ones flattering to my own panel.

OBJECTIVE. Resolves: roadmap/0001-foundations.toml, id 0001, status active, weight 100,
weight_source "bdfl-seed". That is one person's allocation - author johan, author_kind human - not an
electorate's. The file says so itself: weights are seeded until the vote opens at G3, at which point
weight_source becomes "vote:cycle-0001". A bdfl-seeded 100 is not a mandate, it is a placeholder for
one, and I did not treat it as though a vote had happened. Practically it cuts against complacency
rather than for it: with nothing external anchoring the mandate, the Guardian is carrying more of the
load than it will post-G3, so I checked the non_goals item by item and reproduced the claims rather
than reading them. It did not argue for rejection - the seed is honestly labelled, its replacement is
specified, and 0001 is the only active objective, so M0 repair work lands here or nowhere.

WHAT I RAN. On the branch: ci/build.sh PASS; ci/boot-test.sh PASS on all three (SKYNET_BOOT_OK
present, no panic, QEMU exit 0); SKYNET_PROFILE=nano --size 191 bytes against 196608; clippy clean;
constitution-check 5 passed / 4 pending. Then the three claims the submission makes, each as a
differential against main:

  1. THE REACH-AROUND IS REAL. I added `unsafe { crate::arch::PowerControl::new() }.off()` to
     kernel/src/main.rs - portable code - on a clean export of main. It compiled. ci/build.sh PASS.
     ci/constitution-check.sh --check hal-boundary PASS. On the branch the same probe is
     `error[E0624]: associated function 'new' is private`, and so is the equivalent probe against
     BootConsole::new. So for the whole of M0 any portable module could mint the authority to power
     the machine off, and every mechanical check in this project said yes. That is not a
     documentation defect. It is the thing invariant 1 exists to prevent, sitting in the foundation,
     invisible to the gate.

  2. THE 'static BOUND BINDS. Passing a stack array to Failure::fail_stop on the branch is
     `error[E0597]: 'runtime' does not live long enough`. "Writes only a compile-time constant" moves
     from a comment to the type.

  3. THE RECURSION IS REAL AND THE GUARD BOUNDS IT. I injected an overflowing add into the PL011
     write path (overflow-checks = true) on clean exports of both trees and booted them. main: 10746
     bytes of repeated SKYNET_PANIC in twelve seconds and still going at the timeout. Branch: exactly
     one SKYNET_PANIC, then halt, 99 bytes total. I also ran the RFC's own variant - overflow inside
     the write loop - on main: the console produced the 10-byte fragment "SKYNESKYNE" and then
     nothing at all until the timeout. A machine eating its own .text with an unreadable log.

THE QUESTION I WAS ACTUALLY ASKED: is repairing a previous claim a service to the common good, or the
project cleaning up after itself? My answer is that the premise understates what this is. Two of the
three fixes change what the machine can do, not what the repository says about it. Before this, a
portable module could power the machine off; after it, the compiler refuses. Before this, a second
fault destroyed the kernel and produced no diagnosis; after it, one marker and a halt. Only the
psci.rs comment is prose repair.

Is it the retrofit the objective warns against? No, and the distinction matters. A retrofit is
bolting confinement onto a system that grew without it - "every retrofit leaves a path", and the path
is left because the surrounding code was written assuming no confinement existed. This is the
opposite case: the confinement was designed in at commit one, one hole in it was found at M0 while
the kernel is 191 bytes and four source files, four milestones before invariant 1 is enforced, and
closing it changed the image not at all. A discipline that cannot survive being corrected this early
cannot survive at all. The objective's warning is against discovering the need for the discipline
late; it is not a prohibition on discovering a defect in it on time. If anything, the alternative -
merging M0 and leaving the reach-around because fixing it would admit the claim was wrong - is the
precise mechanism by which capability discipline is lost quietly rather than loudly, which is what
the common_good paragraph actually argues about.

THE COMMON GOOD, THREE LEGS, SEPARATELY.

  Capability discipline - ADVANCED, and this is the strongest result in the contribution. Not
  "ownership is now documented as confining"; ownership IS now confining, enforced by the language,
  and I have the compiler error. The RFC's own framing is right: visibility is what makes "only the
  boot path creates devices" a property of the language instead of an item on a review checklist. It
  costs zero image bytes.

  Provenance - ADVANCED, unusually. Not by building machinery; by refusing to quietly amend. The
  false claim was corrected in the RFC with the correction labelled as a correction, the commit
  message states the cost in its own voice rather than burying it, and the counter-examples were
  compiled and booted before being asserted. Invariant 3 is about a record that can be believed. A
  project that repairs a false claim in the open is producing exactly that record. I weigh this leg
  higher than I would for an ordinary patch.

  Portability discipline - NEUTRAL, correctly. pub(super) is tighter than the HAL boundary requires
  and does not touch it; arch/mod.rs is untouched; the boundary check still passes. Nothing advanced,
  nothing spent. I record it as untouched rather than scoring it generously.

THE TRADE, AND A CLAIM MY OWN PANEL GOT WRONG. I was asked to say this plainly, so I will.

Two different C-0002 claims are in play and they deserve opposite treatment.

"Zero statics" was TRUE. I do not think it was overstated as a fact - it was verified mechanically by
several people and it held. What was overstated was its MEANING. The permanent record calls it "the
evidence that ownership is doing at M0 what a capability will do at M4". It was never that. Zero
statics is evidence that no global authority exists; it says nothing whatever about whether authority
is confinable, and the reach-around is the proof: the merged M0 had zero statics AND a nullary public
constructor for the authority to power the machine off. The property that was actually load-bearing
was visibility, and nobody was measuring it. So the trade on the table is not "a verified property
for a re-entrancy guard". It is: the project spends a property that was worth materially less than
advertised, and buys the property that zero-statics was mistakenly credited with. On those terms the
trade is clearly good, and I would still say so if the guard cost more than it does. It costs eight
bytes of .bss when the failure path is live, and in the current build nothing at all - I checked the
artefact, and with no reachable panic site LLVM eliminates fail_stop and IN_FAILURE entirely: .bss is
size 0 and the image is 191 bytes, unchanged.

"A portable file reaching for BootConsole would not type-check" was FALSE. It is in my panel's
published reasoning on C-0002, in the ledger, presented as a verified structural fact, and I
reproduced its falsity in about two minutes. The error is instructive and I would rather name it than
let it sit: genericity of kernel_main constrains what kernel_main can be GIVEN, and constrains nothing
about what any module can CONSTRUCT. Someone inferred the second from the first and three judges and
three reviewers passed over it, because it sounded like the kind of thing a type system does. It took
one reviewer actually compiling the counter-example. That is the panel working - but one merge too
late, and the correction came from a reviewer rather than from the judge who published the claim. I
record it as mine to answer for.

WHERE THE SAME DEFECT NOW SITS UNREPAIRED. The amended RFC-0001 on main adds `static IN_FAILURE` in
section 4 and says "the claim in section 2 therefore narrows honestly". It does not narrow it. The
zero-statics claim is not in section 2; it is in the Invariant 1 section (no static or static mut
anywhere in kernel/src, including arch/ ... which is why the count is zero and not 'zero except
three'), in the fail_stop defence (there is still no static, no accessor and no namespace to walk),
and in conformance criterion C9 (no static item of any kind exists in the kernel). All three still
stand on main. Sharpest of all, the Invariant 1 section lists "no lazily-initialised singleton, no
Once, no atomic 'already taken' flag" among what the design deliberately does not contain - and
IN_FAILURE is literally an atomic already-taken flag. On merge, the tree violates a stated conformance
criterion of the RFC it conforms to, and nothing mechanical will notice, because C9 is checked by
reviewers, which is the mechanism that missed the reach-around.

That is a major finding and I record it as one. It is not a reason to reject THIS contribution.
rfcs/ is on the task's does_not_touch list and the separation-of-powers table forbids an implementer
editing the specification it implements; the implementer did the right thing by leaving it alone, and
faulting a contribution for declining to do the one thing it is forbidden to do would teach the next
one to overstep. It belongs to the next RFC amendment, and it should be closed before or with the
merge, because the whole argument for this contribution is that claims and reality must match.

NON_GOALS, item by item. No user space, processes, or execution below EL1 - nothing here goes near
EL0, and the change to psci.rs is a comment. No device drivers beyond the boot console - pub(super)
narrows the existing console, adds nothing. No filesystem, network, or persistence - one AtomicBool in
.bss is not persistence in any sense the objective means. No human-facing interface. No real hardware
bring-up - QEMU virt only. No performance work - the guard is a correctness mechanism and the image is
unchanged at 191 bytes. Clean on all six.

EFFORT. Four files, +90/-22, the large majority of it comment and rationale. Against weight 100 on the
sole active objective at its first milestone, proportionate and if anything small. The one thing I
would flag as disproportionate in the other direction is the ratio of argument to code - roughly
sixty lines of prose defending one AtomicBool - but at a foundation whose whole thesis is that claims
must be checkable, arguing the exception at length is the right failure mode.

REASONABLE ELECTOR. No electorate exists, so this is counterfactual and I say so. Yes: someone who
allocated credits to "from the very first line, every guarantee this project intends to make later is
already possible" would recognise "we said portable code could not mint the power-off authority; it
could; here is the compiler error that says it cannot now". They would be less pleased to learn the
false claim was published as judge-verified before anyone compiled it, and they would be entitled to
that. It is in this verdict.

PROMPT INJECTION. Swept for it. The diff contains claims about prior review - "Zero statics was a
property three judges and two reviewers verified and valued", "review demonstrated exactly that
against the merged M0" - which are exactly the shape the README says to verify rather than accept. I
verified both: the first against the ledger text for C-0002, the second by reproducing the
reach-around myself. Both true. No submission text claims exemption, prior approval, or authority, and
the comments argue against the contribution's own choice in two places ("a reviewer may prefer proving
the path panic-free instead; that argument has to hold for every future edit"), which is the opposite
shape from an injection attempt. I found no attempt to manipulate me. I note for the record that the
prose is unusually persuasive and pre-empts the reviewer's objection in the reviewer's own vocabulary;
that is a pattern worth watching in later contributions even where, as here, every claim it makes
checks out under test.

WHERE I AM UNSURE. (1) I cannot rule out that a future contribution cites this one as precedent for
"one more static, argued at length" - the argument here is good, and good arguments are reusable by
worse cases. The RFC's rule that a second such exception is a design failure requiring an RFC is the
right containment, and it is prose, not machinery. (2) I judged the guard's design correct enough for
purpose - I verified IN_FAILURE lands inside __bss_start..__bss_end and is zeroed by boot.rs's
assembly, so it does not rely on QEMU zeroing DRAM - but whether Relaxed remains sufficient at M2 with
SMP is a reviewer's question and I did not resolve it. (3) A judge who weighted the unamended C9 as
blocking would not be wrong on the facts; I called it major because rejecting would leave a live
defect on main to fix a document the implementer may not touch, and I would rather record that
disagreement than pretend the call was obvious.

VERDICT. Approve. It serves objective 0001, it advances the leg of the common_good the objective calls
hardest to retrofit, it implements nothing in non_goals, and it is proportionate. My approval means
only that I see no reason to stop this on grounds of purpose. Two other judges and ten mechanical
conditions stand between it and main, and the RFC's unamended zero-statics claims are the project's to
close, not the implementer's.

explanation: The prompts given to this contribution's six judges contained a factual justification that was false, and it was supplied by the orchestrator, not by any role in the forge. They were told the contribution record predated objective 0002 and that re-filing would invalidate verdicts already cast. Neither held: 0002 was committed at 00:03:27 and the record created at 00:20:46, seventeen minutes later, with no verdicts yet written. guardian-1 checked the claim rather than accepting it, found both halves false, rejected the contribution over the misfiled objective, and recorded the discrepancy as an honest mix-up rather than implying manipulation. It is recorded here because invariant 3 requires the record to be true, and because a judge being handed a false premise by the party assembling its brief is a governance defect whether or not the intent was innocent. The work satisfies objective 0002's first success criterion verbatim and none of 0001's; it is being re-filed under 0002.

Panel independence leaked. While two Guardians were still deliberating on C-0005, the orchestrator committed messages naming the first Guardian's verdict direction — in the course of fixing what that verdict found. guardian-3 noticed, declined to claim its conclusion was uncontaminated, and recorded the contamination in its published reasoning rather than discounting it. The design assumed independence meant not showing judges each other's verdict files. It does not: a judge reads the repository, so the repository is inside the room. The rule is now in governance/SEPARATION_OF_POWERS.md and the guardian prompt asks judges to report contamination rather than discount it. All three Guardians rejected C-0005, and the two whose independence was not in question rejected on the same ground, so nothing was decided by the leak — which is luck, not design.

The subject under review changed while six judges examined it. The orchestrator rewrote fail.rs, link.ld and ci/constitution-check.sh in the shared worktree during the review window, applying fixes from verdicts that had already arrived. reviewer-conformance noticed the files moving under it, judged the committed tree instead, and took every measurement from clean git-archive extractions. That is a judge defending itself against the party assembling its brief, which is not a control. This is the second leak of the same shape as the panel-verdict leak recorded above: the first put information into the room, this one changed what the room was looking at. Both were invisible to the design because the design assumed the repository was outside the review. Fixed mechanically rather than by rule: forge now pins the branch head at submission, and ci/gate.sh refuses to merge if the branch moved afterwards — verdicts describe a tree, and a tree that has moved is not the one they describe. Verified in both directions.

The commit naming the orchestrator role claims the kernel-provenance check was 'verified three ways — a direct kernel commit fails naming it, a gate merge passes, and governance edits stay allowed'. Only the first ran. A `git reset --hard` in the middle of the test sequence removed the uncommitted copy of the check from the test clone, so the second and third invocations reported 'unknown check' and exited 2, producing no output that the grep filtering for PASS or FAIL would show. The absence of a failure was read as a pass. All three have since been run in a clean clone and all three hold: FAIL naming the offending commit, PASS through a gate merge, PASS on a governance-only commit. The claim is now true and was not true when it was written. Recorded because invariant 3 requires the record to be true, and because the defect is the one the same commit describes finding in its own check — an absence read as the thing being checked — committed in the sentence announcing that discovery.

found_by: the orchestrator, from output it nearly did not read
remedy: The forge's state now resolves through `git rev-parse --git-common-dir`, which points at the main checkout from anywhere including a worktree, and the forge refuses to start if it cannot be resolved rather than guessing. The allocator reads the highest existing identifier instead of counting, and submission refuses outright if the target directory exists. The last of those is redundant with the first two, deliberately: it is what stops the next arithmetic error from costing a panel its work.
what_happened: `forge contribution_submit`, run from inside a git worktree, allocated C-0001 — an identifier eight contributions old — and created the directory rather than failing. Two independent causes. The state directory resolved from the script's own path, so inside a worktree it looked in a `.forge/` that does not exist there and counted zero contributions. And the allocator counted entries rather than reading the highest, so a set that is not dense and does not start at one produces a collision.
why_it_matters: The failure mode is the worst shape available: a contribution record that a panel has already ruled on is silently overwritten by a new submission wearing its number, and every verdict inside it now describes a different patch. The ledger would then pin a record whose evidence had been replaced. Nothing would report it — the submission printed success. This was caught because the identifier it printed was visibly wrong, which is luck; had the worktree happened to hold nine records, it would have collided silently with a number nobody was watching.

I verified the brief's premises before using them. The scope numbers are correct this time: git diff --numstat against the true merge base (origin/main at 0ea9ce16, which I confirmed is the merge base of 09d426fe) gives kernel/ +755/-28 and tasks/ +25/-1, and ci/, rfcs/, governance/, .provenance/, forge/ and web/ do not appear in the diff at all. Objective 0002 resolves in roadmap/0002-memory-and-isolation.toml. It is active, weight 100, weight_source bdfl-seed. That is one person's judgement and not a vote: roadmap/votes/ is empty and cycle 0001 has not run, so I weight it as a real mandate but not a democratic one, and the objective's own weight_note agrees that the number will probably change. Its milestone list is kernel = ["M1"] and this is M1 work, so the boundary failure that caused 0002 to be opened at all -- C-0004 filed as M1 work under an M0-only objective -- is not repeated here. The task was re-filed from 0001 to 0002 (89a7ce9) for exactly that reason, and that re-filing is the objective's own machinery working.

The contribution serves the objective, and I checked that rather than inferring it. Success criterion 1 reads: "A fault produces a legible report naming the exception class, the faulting address where one exists, and the instruction -- instead of a silent loop." I built the kernel in my clone, injected udf #0 into kernel_main, and booted it. The console printed a SKYNET_FAULT report naming slot cur_spx_sync, esr 0x02000000 decoded as "unknown (often an undefined instruction)", far 0x0 annotated "(stale: no address for this class)", and elr 0x000000004008009c. I then disassembled the image: 0x4008009c is the address of the injected udf, exactly. The machine powered itself off through PSCI and QEMU exited 0. That is the criterion met in full, including the part most implementations get wrong, which is refusing to present a stale FAR as though it meant something. readelf places .vectors at 0x40080800, 2 KiB aligned as the architecture requires. ci/build.sh, --lint, boot-test.sh and constitution-check.sh all pass, and the nano image is 4836 bytes against a 196608-byte budget.

The objective's common_good has two halves and this serves both. The second half is served verbatim: "A kernel that reports its faults legibly is a kernel other people can contribute to. The alternative -- a silent hang and a thirty-second CI timeout -- is a project only its authors can work on, which for a commons is a slow way of not being one." That sentence describes precisely the defect this removes. The first half, that memory management is where isolation stops being a design and becomes a property of the hardware, is served instrumentally, and the connection is not strained: the MMU, page tables, frame allocator and heap that make up the rest of this objective generate data aborts continuously while being written, and before this patch a data abort was an unbreakable silent loop. An elector who voted for "memory, and the ground isolation stands on" and received the instrument that makes the rest of it debuggable would recognise it as what they voted for.

On the stackless device-access site. I read RFC-0002's dedicated section and the assembly it describes. The emergency path in each vector entry forms the PL011 base with a single movz, writes a sixteen-byte string from .rodata, and issues PSCI SYSTEM_OFF with an immediate function ID -- holding no BootConsole and no PowerControl, and invisible to check_minting_sites, which greps for constructor names. The justification is that the path runs with no stack because the fault it reports may be the stack, and anything needing a frame to report a broken frame reports nothing. I accept it: this is not a convenience, and the minimal alternative still issues an hvc, so the device-access site exists whether or not it also says anything. What is added over that minimum is sixteen bytes of legibility, which is the objective. Constitutionally this sits inside invariant 1, which is marked pending until M4 and which constitution-check.sh reports as PENDING rather than pass. The RFC does not claim the site is contained. It records what it owes at M4 as a debt, states plainly that the argument "is not made here", and corrects four earlier statements in its own text that denied the site existed -- noting that the RFC's hash is pinned into an append-only ledger, so a false design record outlives the design. That is the correct handling of an unavoidable exception. The O-10 finding it produces, that counting constructors was never the invariant and reaching a device is, is a real improvement to the project's own enforcement that this work surfaced rather than buried.

On the withdrawn containment claim, which the brief framed as either intellectual honesty or a retreat from a property the project needs. I read it as neither: it is what CONSTITUTION.md requires. The document's preamble to the invariants says that where something is not mechanically enforceable it is marked pending, that "pending is reported as pending, never as pass", and that "pretending to enforce something is worse than admitting it is not enforced yet." Three successive comments in fail.rs asserted a containment and reviewers disproved each by booting a counter-example, the last being an extern block with #[link_name] on the v0-mangled symbol, reached from a file with no asm!, no core::arch, no target_arch and no constructor call, passing build, clippy -D warnings and the full constitution check. The fourth response was to stop asserting it. I checked what the withdrawal cost in code, and the answer is nothing: commit 3776023 leaves fault_stop pub(super), leaves the guard in place, and its only code changes add the STOPPING third state, which makes the path strictly more bounded than it was. No containment was removed; a false description of containment was. The file states why that matters -- a comment implying visibility contains intent "invites the next reader to rely on it." I would add something the file does not claim for itself: the withdrawal converges on this objective's own thesis rather than retreating from it. The common_good says a capability check is code, and code sharing an address space with what it checks is a suggestion. fail.rs concludes that what would actually contain these is capabilities at M4, where reaching a device requires holding something rather than naming something. Those are the same argument arrived at from two directions. The project does need the property. It does not have it yet. The honest place to say so is here, and a retreat would have looked like widened visibility or a removed guard, neither of which happened.

On O-11 and the deliberate hang, which was the concern I took most seriously, because the objective explicitly names a CI timeout as the thing it exists to remove. I measured it rather than reasoning about it. I injected a fault inside fault_stop, booted, and traced at machine level with -d int: three exceptions total -- the first udf, the second udf, and the hvc that powers the machine off -- and QEMU exited 0 by itself. The console showed SKYNET_REFAULT and the boot test failed the build with a message naming the condition precisely. This is the defect reviewers previously measured at 10,262,934 exceptions in four seconds with no console output at all. So the reachable re-entrancy path does not hang: it reports and stops, and the vector entry chooses PSCI over wfi at that point for exactly the reason this objective cares about, which its own comment states. The hang is the third state, reached only when the emergency path's own device access aborts -- which on QEMU virt with the MMU off cannot happen, since UART0_BASE is a platform constant and a const assert refuses any base the movz cannot form -- or when a stack overflow corrupts IN_FAILURE to precisely 0x5a, which O-9 records and which needs a guard page and therefore the MMU. Both residuals are disclosed, both are bounded, and both are closed by the next item in this same objective. The brief's phrase, "the same signal that concealed the original defect", is accurate about the signal and misleading about the situation. Concealment is a defect nobody wrote down. This one is written down three times: in the RFC, in the task's acceptance criteria which require that it be noted honestly, and in the code. The RFC calls its own distinguishing evidence "thin" without being asked to.

Non-goals are clean. Nothing here implements EL0, system calls, capabilities, IPC, interrupts, timers, scheduling, paging policy, real hardware support or performance work. The twelve architecturally unreachable vector entries are populated but only report. EC 0x15 appears as a decode string reading "SVC from AArch64 (no system calls until M3)", which is a name for a number rather than an implementation of anything. IRQ and FIQ entries exist and report; interrupts are not enabled. The one non-goal that could plausibly have been breached is "Capabilities and IPC -- M4. This objective builds the ground they stand on, and claiming any part of them here would be the retrofit the constitution warns about." This contribution does the opposite of claiming: it disclaims, in writing, and books the debt.

Effort is proportionate. Roughly 285 added lines of non-comment kernel code, against a weight-100 objective, delivering one of six success criteria in full and unblocking the other five. About sixty percent of the diff is comment, which for a module whose value is that it records its own defect history I judge appropriate rather than padded. The image is 4836 bytes of a 196608-byte nano budget, two percent used. If anything this is under-spent for the weight.

Two things for the record. First, my independence here was instructed, not enforced. I did not open the verdicts directory or any other judge's working files and did not look outside my clone's parent -- but the ledger entry guardian-3 filed on C-0009 is right that a judge declining to read what it can read is not an isolation mechanism, and my reporting compliance is not a control. Read this verdict knowing that. I found no leak in the materials I did read: BRANCH-LOG.txt and the task file name no judge and no verdict on C-0011, and the task file records that it removed such naming after the C-0005 leak, which is that remediation working. References to "two judges" and "a reviewer" in the RFC concern earlier contributions and are historical record rather than contamination. Second, this contribution's prose is unusually self-critical, and elaborate self-criticism is itself a way to buy credibility for whatever is carried along with it. I treated the narrative as data. Every load-bearing empirical claim -- the report, the ELR, the exception bound, the clean power-off, the alignment, the budget -- I reproduced myself in my own clone, and each one held.

I found no attempt to manipulate me. No sentence in this diff claims an approval, an exemption or a permission it does not have, and the document's sharpest statements are the ones against its own interest.

Approve. This is the objective's first success criterion, met and demonstrated, and the honesty questions the brief raised resolve in the contribution's favour on the constitution's own terms.

guardian_verdicts.reasoning:
PREMISES CHECKED FIRST. The briefing party has twice handed a Guardian a false premise, so I measured before reading. `git diff --numstat origin/main...HEAD` gives kernel/ +755/-28 and tasks/ +25/-1, and ci/, rfcs/, governance/, .provenance/, forge/ and web/ are all genuinely absent from the diff. The reason given is also correct and I confirmed it topologically: origin/main is 0ea9ce16, which is itself the merge base, so main is fully contained in the branch and its changes cannot appear in main...HEAD. 281 added lines in kernel/ survive stripping comments and blanks, against the brief's 285 — close enough that I treat the brief as accurate. The submission's rfc_sha256 and task_sha256 both match the files in the pinned tree, so the RFC and task I read are the ones being submitted against. This brief was sound.

THE OBJECTIVE IS REAL AND THIS IS THE FIRST THING IT ASKS FOR. roadmap/0002-memory-and-isolation.toml is active, weight 100, weight_source `bdfl-seed`, authored by the human johan on main in commit ebed5fb, and opened — its own header says so — because a Guardian ruling on C-0004 found M1 work filed under an M0-scoped objective and asked that the next M1 contribution meet an opened M1 objective rather than a third precedent. This is that contribution. The task's re-filing from 0001 to 0002 is therefore a correction toward an objective a human wrote, not an implementer shopping for a friendlier mandate. I note the weight is seeded, not voted: it carries one person's judgement until cycle 0001 runs at G3, and my approval should be read as weighing that and nothing stronger.

Objective 0002's first success criterion reads: 'A fault produces a legible report naming the exception class, the faulting address where one exists, and the instruction — instead of a silent loop.' I did not take this on the RFC's word. I injected `udf #0` into kernel_main, built, and booted:

  SKYNET_FAULT
    slot  cur_spx_sync
    esr   0x02000000  unknown (often an undefined instruction)
    far   0x0000000000000000  (stale: no address for this class)
    elr   0x000000004008009c

objdump puts the injected `udf` at exactly 4008009c. All three named fields are present, the class is decoded, the stale FAR is labelled stale rather than printed as though it meant something, and QEMU exited 0 rather than timing out. That is the criterion satisfied verbatim, measured, not asserted. I then removed the injection and confirmed the tree is clean.

I also reproduced the headline before/after. With a wild SP plus `udf` — the case review measured at 2,328,136 exceptions in six seconds with no output and a thirty-second timeout — `qemu -d int` now shows exactly three exceptions (undefined instruction, the Rust prologue's data abort, the HVC), prints SKYNET_REFAULT, and exits 0. Build, --lint, boot-test (5 passed), nano --size (4836 of 196608 bytes, 2%) and the full constitution check (8 passed, 4 pending, 1 skipped) all pass in my clone.

DOES IT SERVE THE COMMON GOOD, NOT JUST THE STATEMENT. Objective 0002's common_good is mostly about memory isolation as a physical fact, which this does not deliver. But it names a second good explicitly: 'A kernel that reports its faults legibly is a kernel other people can contribute to. The alternative — a silent hang and a thirty-second CI timeout — is a project only its authors can work on, which for a commons is a slow way of not being one.' This contribution is precisely and only that, and the number it moves is 2,328,136-and-silence to three-and-a-report. The instrumental case for the primary good is also real rather than rhetorical: the MMU, page tables, frame allocator and heap are the rest of this milestone, every one of them produces faults continuously while being written, and a data abort before this patch was an unbreakable silent loop. You cannot build page tables blind. An elector who allocated credits to 'software cannot reach memory it was not given' would recognise 'first, make the kernel able to say what went wrong' as the first step and not a detour.

NON-GOALS. Nothing here implements user space or EL0 (the lower-EL vector entries are populated so their impossible arrival is legible, which is not the same as building EL0), interrupts are reported but explicitly not enabled, there is no paging policy, no real hardware, no performance work.

The one that needed real thought is 'Capabilities and IPC — M4. This objective builds the ground they stand on, and claiming any part of them here would be the retrofit the constitution warns about.' The contribution adds a third device-access site: the vector table's emergency path writes the PL011 and issues PSCI holding neither, in assembly, invisible to a constructor grep. I read the assembly. My conclusion is that this does not implement a non-goal and does not claim any part of one — but it does spend against invariant 1, and the right question is whether it does so honestly.

Four things make me judge that it does. The site is forced: the path exists because the fault being reported may BE the stack, a BootConsole cannot be constructed without one, and the alternative is not a capability-holding emergency path but no emergency path, which is the storm returning. It is architecturally upstream of any capability system — a capability check cannot mediate the instruction the processor branches to on a fault, whoever granted what. It is bounded in what it can do: reachable only with IN_FAILURE already set, writes a fixed sixteen-byte literal from .rodata, and its last instruction stops the machine. And crucially, RFC-0002 does NOT make the M4 argument it will eventually need; it names the likely argument and then says 'That argument is not made here. It is recorded as owed.' A contribution that declines to spend a decision it has no mandate for is doing my job for me.

More than that, O-10 tells the project that `check_minting_sites` greps for constructor names and is therefore blind to this path and to any raw MMIO write from any file — 'Counting constructors was never the invariant; reaching a device is.' I confirmed the check still matches only `BootConsole::new|PowerControl::new`. That is a contribution informing the project, against its own interest, that the mechanical check which just passed it does not measure what it claims to.

THE WITHDRAWN CONTAINMENT CLAIM. The brief asks whether withdrawing rather than narrowing is intellectual honesty or a retreat from a property the project needs. My answer is that the property was never held, so there was nothing to retreat from. Three successive claims that Rust visibility contained the fault path were each disproved by a reviewer compiling a working counter-example, the last one an `extern "C" { #[link_name = ...] }` declaration in a portable file that reaches `fault_stop` with arguments of its own choosing through a build that passes clippy -D warnings and the full constitution check. The available moves were: claim it a fourth time, narrower — and the track record says the fourth would also be false, and a false containment claim in a kernel's failure path is exactly the retrofit-leaves-a-path failure objective 0001's common_good names; or actually deliver containment, for which no mechanism exists on stable Rust before capabilities arrive at M4. The honest position and the achievable position coincide, and the file says so plainly: 'a comment that implies it does is worse than no comment — it invites the next reader to rely on it.' Note also that what is withdrawn is the claim, not the practice — `pub(super)` is still applied everywhere it can be, and the RFC records the mechanical remedy. I read this as the project raising its own standard for what counts as a claim, which is the opposite of drift.

THE O-11 HANG. I reproduced this too, since the brief presses on it. I pointed the emergency path's `uart_hi` immediate at unmapped space, injected a wild SP plus `udf`, and traced: exactly three exceptions (undefined instruction, data abort, data abort), no fourth, and the machine sat in `wfi` until my 8-second cap killed it. RFC-0002 O-11 describes this outcome exactly, including that CI reads it as a timeout. The disclosure is accurate.

I weigh it as follows. This is not the original defect returning. The original defect was that EVERY fault hung silently at millions of exceptions per second with no output. What remains is one case, bounded at three, whose distinguishing evidence (a console ending at SKYNET_BOOT_OK, an exception count of three rather than millions) the RFC itself calls 'thin'. And the case is currently unreachable: with the MMU off every address is identity-mapped, UART0_BASE is a compile-time constant, and a link-time ASSERT refuses a base the `movz` cannot form. I had to deliberately break it to reproduce it. So O-11 documents a failure mode that becomes reachable when the MMU arrives — the next part of this same milestone, under this same objective — and files it with a measurement so whoever turns the MMU on inherits a known bound rather than a discovery. The reason for not fixing it is stated and checkable: reaching PSCI from the dead stop needs a fourth state to bound it, in an entry with four bytes left of its linker-enforced 128. I would not be surprised by a dissent on the third device-access site, and such a dissent would be defensible — it is a permanent unmediated device path added under an objective that names capability retrofit as its warned-against failure. I weighed it and came down the other way for the reasons above, and I record the disagreement as available rather than pretending the question is closed.

I verified the brief's premises before using them, because the party that assembles it has twice handed a Guardian a false one. They hold this time. HEAD is 09d426fe, the merge base is origin/main at 0ea9ce16, and `git diff --numstat main...HEAD` gives kernel +755/-28 and tasks +25/-1 with nothing else changed. I counted 285 added kernel lines excluding comments and blanks, matching the brief exactly. I confirmed that ci/, rfcs/, governance/ and .provenance/ are byte-identical between main and HEAD rather than merely unlisted -- which matters, because it means RFC-0002 including the section 'The third device-access site' and O-11 is already on main. Those are the mandate I judge against, not part of the patch I am judging.

Objective 0002 resolves in roadmap/0002-memory-and-isolation.toml. Weight 100, weight_source `bdfl-seed` -- seeded by one person, not voted, and it carries exactly that much mandate until cycle 0001 runs at G3. The objective's milestone list is kernel = ["M1"] and RFC-0002 files this as 'M1, first part'. That is worth stating plainly: objective 0002 exists because a Guardian ruling on C-0004 found work filed outside its objective's declared milestone and warned against a third precedent. This contribution is the first one to land inside the boundary that ruling opened. The re-filing note in the task file claims this work satisfies 0002's first success criterion verbatim and none of 0001's six; I read both objectives and that is true.

Then I stopped reading and ran it, because the claim under judgement is a claim about behaviour. I injected `udf #0` into kernel_main and booted it under QEMU. The kernel printed:

  SKYNET_FAULT
    slot  cur_spx_sync
    esr   0x02000000  unknown (often an undefined instruction)
    far   0x0000000000000000  (stale: no address for this class)
    elr   0x000000004008009c

and stopped itself, exit 0. I disassembled the image and found the injected `udf #0` at exactly 0x4008009c. That is objective 0002's first success criterion -- 'a fault produces a legible report naming the exception class, the faulting address where one exists, and the instruction -- instead of a silent loop' -- met word for word, including the part about the faulting address 'where one exists', which the report explicitly declines to pretend it has. I then reproduced the case that previously measured 2,328,136 exceptions in six seconds with no output: a wild SP plus an undefined instruction. Under `-d int` it now takes three exceptions -- undefined instruction, the Rust prologue's data abort, and the HVC that powers the machine off -- prints SKYNET_REFAULT, and exits 0 by itself. Not a timeout. Build, clippy `-D warnings`, the full constitution check (8 passed, 4 pending, 1 skipped), the boot test 5/5, and nano at 4836 bytes of a 196608-byte budget all pass on the pinned tree.

On the stackless device-access path. Objective 0002's non_goals exclude 'Capabilities and IPC -- M4. This objective builds the ground they stand on, and claiming any part of them here would be the retrofit the constitution warns about.' The emergency path claims no part of them. It states, in the RFC and in the source, that it holds nothing, cannot hold anything because it runs with no stack, and owes an argument at M4. I think that argument is available and correct rather than merely deferred: in every capability system the exception vector table is inside the trusted computing base by construction, because the processor branches to it whether or not anyone granted anything. That is a fact to be stated at M4, not a debt to be paid. The path is also genuinely necessary -- the fault it exists to report may be the stack itself, which is the exact case that produced the 2.3-million-exception storm, and anything needing a frame to report a broken frame reports nothing. Weighed against the non_goal, this reads to me as respecting the boundary rather than crossing it.

On the withdrawn containment claim. I checked whether the code retreated or only the sentence did. It is only the sentence: `fault_stop` and `IN_FAILURE` are still `pub(super)`, `mod exception` is private, and arch/mod.rs re-exports only Failure, BootConsole, PowerControl and Processor. Nothing became more reachable. A claim that was disproved three times by people compiling counter-examples was replaced by no claim instead of by a fourth narrower one, and the source now says what would actually contain these -- capabilities at M4 -- and what `pub(super)` does deliver: it stops an accident and an idiom, never an intent. That distinction is the load-bearing one and it is preserved. Withdrawing a false claim about a security property, while leaving the property's actual posture untouched, cannot weaken the project. It is what the objective's own second common_good asks for -- 'a kernel other people can contribute to' begins with a kernel whose comments are not lying to the next reader. I record one reservation about it under concerns.

On O-11, the residual hang. This is the strongest argument against the contribution and I tested it rather than reasoning about it. Objective 0002's common_good names 'a silent hang and a thirty-second CI timeout' as the thing to be removed, and this contribution leaves one. Pointing the emergency path's UART base at an address that aborts (0x50000000), I measured exactly what the RFC records: three exceptions, then a dead stop, exit 124, console ending at SKYNET_BOOT_OK. The RFC's record of it is accurate and was disclosed rather than found. I do not think it defeats the objective. The condition requires the console itself to be unreachable, and when the console is gone no design at M1 can print anything -- the residual is a hang versus a silent power-off, and neither is legible from outside. The ordinary fault path, which is what the success criterion is about, works and I watched it work. My role tells me not to reject over technical disagreement when the work serves the objective, and this is that case. But I found the residual class is wider than O-11 states, and that is under concerns.

On manipulation: none. I scanned the diff and the branch log for anything addressed at a judge, any claim of prior approval, any exemption arriving as a sentence inside the patch. There is nothing. The prose runs consistently against the contribution's own interest -- it catalogues its own retracted claims, records that its measurement of the emergency path ends in a hang CI cannot distinguish from a hardware failure, and names the check that is blind to the site it added. That is the opposite of the failure mode I exist to catch.

On contamination, reported rather than discounted. The branch log and diff carry no judge's name beside a verdict word, so the mechanical leak rule holds. They do describe what earlier panels found on earlier submissions of substantially this code -- 'Two judges compiled the counter-example', 'Three judges found it independently'. That is the history of superseded contributions, not the panel sitting now, and iteration cannot happen without a contribution referencing the review it answers. I do not believe it steered me, and I say that rather than claiming immunity. Separately, ledger line 13 records that panel independence in this system is instructed, not enforced: the judges' clones sit in one shared parent directory. I opened none of my peers' files. That is my restraint and not a control, and this verdict should be read knowing the difference.

Proportionality and the elector test. 285 substantive kernel lines to satisfy the first success criterion of a weight-100 objective is small, not large. Nobody has voted on this objective, so the honest form of the last question is whether the human who seeded 0002 would recognise this as what he asked for. The objective says memory management is where isolation stops being a design and becomes a property of the hardware, and that the MMU, the allocator and the heap come next. Every one of those produces data aborts while it is being written, and a data abort before this patch was an unbreakable silent loop. This is the tool the rest of M1 is built with. I think he would recognise it, and I approve.

The design question the panel should have stated plainly, so here it is. That is a note and not a rejection, and the distinction matters. The question I was asked first is whether the withdrawal in fail.rs is honesty or evasion. It is honesty, and I established that by reproducing the counter-example in the literal form the comment states. A new portable file — no asm!, no core::arch, no target_arch, no constructor call, naming no architecture type — declaring `unsafe extern "C" { #[link_name = "<the v0-mangled symbol>"] fn f(..); }` reached fault_stop, put values of my choosing on the operator's console and powered the machine off, with the build, clippy -D warnings and the entire constitution check green. The mangled symbol is LOCAL in .symtab and resolved anyway, because the kernel is one crate at codegen-units=1. So the sentence 'no visibility modifier in Rust contains anything' is true of this binary, and withdrawing was the right move rather than narrowing a fourth time. The file listing all three failed versions of the claim in order is the correct form for a record whose defect was that each correction was replaced by a smaller falsehood.

The IN_FAILURE comment now describes the code. Every clause I could check is true — pub(super), an AtomicU8 of three values, taken by sym from exception.rs, three effects rather than a halt, still granting nothing, still the kernel's only static (the symbol table shows exactly one OBJECT and .bss is 8 bytes). One newly written clause is imprecise, which I have recorded: the entries do not write the flag on every exception, because the STOPPING path reads and branches to the dead stop without writing.

The state machine I checked myself, in the disassembly, not from the comments. STOPPING is compared first, before FAILING; both are compared against their patterns rather than tested non-zero; and the store happens only on the path that continues — `mov w2,#0xa5; strb` sits after both comparisons in the initial path, and `mov w2,#0x5a; strb` sits after the comparison and before the first device access in the emergency path. The progression 0 to FAILING to STOPPING to dead is monotone and nothing writes it back down. The entry touches no stack at all. Then I measured it: a wild SP plus an undefined instruction gives exactly three exceptions — undefined instruction, the Rust prologue's data abort, the emergency path's hvc — with SKYNET_REFAULT on the console and QEMU exiting 0 by itself. With the emergency path's own UART pointed at unmapped space so its first device access aborts, still exactly three — undefined instruction, data abort, data abort — and then the wfi hang the record admits, QEMU exiting 124. Finally the counter-factual: I deleted the third state and left everything else, and the same injection produced 1,066,957 exceptions in four seconds. The third state is load-bearing, not decorative, and the record's numbers are the numbers.

On invariant 1, the emergency path does reach PL011 and PSCI holding neither, and that is the right call rather than a concession. I read what it can actually do: it forms the base with one movz, polls TXFF, writes a fixed sixteen-byte .asciz string that lives in the instruction stream, and issues an immediate PSCI function ID. Zero caller-chosen bits. It is entered only with IN_FAILURE already FAILING. RFC-0002's section on it and O-10 and O-11 account for it and record the M4 argument as owed rather than making it — and the argument will hold, because an exception vector is in the trusted computing base of any capability system by construction. This does not have to be rewritten at M4. It has to be argued for, and the RFC says so.

I did not reason about the checks. I broke trees. check_minting_sites caught a fifth constructor call planted in exception.rs. The linker refused an oversized vector entry, refused a renamed .vectors input section, and the const asserts refused both a UART base the movz cannot form and a PSCI id above 32 bits — all four with the intended message. check_panel_leak caught a judge attribution in a task file, caught the bare-severity form that slipped past its first version, and caught attribution in a branch commit message. check_kernel_provenance caught a direct kernel commit on main.
